title: 21 Jump Street
logline: Two cops go undercover at a high school. Self-aware action comedy.
overview: When cops Schmidt and Jenko join the secret Jump Street unit, they use their youthful appearances to go undercover as high school students. They trade in their guns and badges for backpacks, and set out to shut down a dangerous drug ring. But, as time goes on, Schmidt and Jenko discover that high school is nothing like it was just a few years earlier -- and, what's more, they must again confront the teenage terror and anxiety they thought they had left behind.
tagline: The only thing getting blown tonight is their cover.

jokes.text: Jenko's botched prom ask — he stammers, clearly building to asking Melodie to prom, and she cuts him off horrified
jokes.setup: Jenko nervously says they've known each other for a long time, live across the street, and prom is in four days — classic romantic buildup
jokes.punchline: She panics: 'Oh my God. You're not asking me to prom, are you?' — confirming the audience's read and immediately deflating him
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe setup that efficiently establishes Jenko as a popular but socially oblivious jock. The horror on her face is the punchline — the audience sees exactly what's coming which gives it a cringe-anticipation quality. Not especially original but executed cleanly.

jokes.text: 'Fuck, no. No, I... No, I just...' — Jenko's overcorrection after she asks if he's asking her to prom
jokes.setup: She's horrified at the thought of him asking her to prom
jokes.punchline: His immediate and emphatic 'Fuck, no' — desperate to save face — is funnier than any romantic rejection would have been
jokes.explanation: The speed and vehemence of the denial is perfectly timed — Channing Tatum's delivery makes it land. It flips the cringe: now HE's the one embarrassed in reverse. Good character work showing Jenko's ego over genuine feeling.

jokes.text: 'You're a fucking nerd.' Jenko tells the girl he WAS trying to ask out about another girl who is 'hot.' 'Look at her. Look at her. Look at her. Look at her.'
jokes.setup: Melodie tries to let him down easy after the botched prom attempt
jokes.punchline: Instead of retreating gracefully, Jenko doubles down, calling her a nerd and obsessively pointing out a hot girl, repeating 'Look at her' like a golden retriever spotting a squirrel
jokes.explanation: The repeated 'Look at her' escalation is what elevates this from a simple insult joke. Jenko's total lack of self-awareness is the engine of this film's comedy, and this is an efficient early demonstration of it. The escalation into dog-like repetition is genuinely funny.

jokes.text: Jenko's repeated 'Look at her. Look at her. Look at her. Look at her. Look at her.' while pointing at the hot girl
jokes.setup: Melodie has just pointed out a hot girl as the reason Schmidt isn't worth dating
jokes.punchline: Jenko piles on with five consecutive 'Look at her' repetitions — the escalation of agreement makes it funnier than a single 'look at her' would
jokes.explanation: The repetition escalation works modestly — it characterizes Jenko as oblivious and lecherous, and the rhythm of the repeated phrase is funny. Not a great joke on its own but good world-building for his character.

jokes.text: Principal tells Jenko he has to 'pay the piper.' Jenko responds: 'I should pay who?'
jokes.setup: Principal uses the idiom 'pay the piper' as a dramatic warning
jokes.punchline: Jenko takes it literally — he genuinely doesn't know the expression — perfectly illustrating his academic failures
jokes.explanation: Very economical character joke. Three words that do double duty: establish Jenko as genuinely uneducated (not just slacker cool) and deliver a clean laugh. The literal interpretation of the idiom is a reliable structure but it fits the character perfectly here.

jokes.text: 'But I'm going to be prom king.' / 'I'm glad you had a great time in school. 'Cause you ain't learned nothing.'
jokes.setup: Principal tells Jenko he's not going to prom — the consequence for bad grades
jokes.punchline: Jenko's delusional insistence that he'll be prom king, followed by the principal's withering summary of his entire academic career
jokes.explanation: The principal's capping line 'you ain't learned nothing' is a nice double-meaning (grammar joke embedded in content) that works efficiently. Jenko's delusion is consistent character work. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Jenko spots Schmidt at the police academy: 'Not-so-slim Shady, what's up? Holy shit!'
jokes.setup: High school bully Jenko arrives at the police academy and runs into the nerd he used to torment
jokes.punchline: His nickname 'Not-so-slim Shady' instantly conveys that Schmidt was an overweight Eminem-wannabe in high school — a dense, funny character detail delivered in four words
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy — 'Not-so-slim Shady' tells us Schmidt was fat, tried to be cool by emulating Eminem, and failed at both. It recontextualizes the earlier 'fucking nerd' characterization and implies a whole humiliating backstory in a single nickname. This is efficient, specific, funny writing.

jokes.text: Schmidt, clearly struggling at physical police training, is complimented by Jenko: 'You're really good at this.' Schmidt: 'Yeah, I am.' Jenko: 'Hey, you want to be friends?'
jokes.setup: Schmidt, the academic nerd, is performing well at something physical — which surprises Jenko, the former cool jock who is apparently struggling
jokes.punchline: Jenko's offer of friendship is transactional — a popular kid condescending to befriend the nerd because he now needs him. 'Hey, you want to be friends?' lands as pathetically eager from someone who used to bully Schmidt.
jokes.explanation: Good role-reversal comedy — the former bully now needs the nerd. The delivery of 'Hey, you want to be friends?' is what makes it work: it's sincere and slightly desperate, which is funnier than if it were sarcastic. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: 'I really thought this job would have more car chases and explosions, and less homeless people doo-dooing everywhere.'
jokes.setup: Schmidt and Jenko have graduated the police academy and are now assigned to... park duty
jokes.punchline: Schmidt's disappointment expressed through the contrast of action-movie expectations vs. the word 'doo-dooing' — a childish euphemism that undercuts any attempt at hardboiled cop talk
jokes.explanation: The word 'doo-dooing' is doing significant work here. The contrast between 'car chases and explosions' (cinematic cop fantasy) and the mundane, childishly-phrased reality is funny, and 'doo-dooing' specifically is a perfect word choice — Schmidt is a nerd-cop who can't even commit to adult profanity. Good line.

jokes.text: Two rookie cops responding to a Frisbee complaint: 'Do you guys really think this is a police matter? To get your Frisbee back?' / 'Get your own fucking Frisbee.'
jokes.setup: Fresh academy graduates are deployed as park police — the most unglamorous possible assignment
jokes.punchline: Jenko's complete contempt for the civilians they're meant to serve, dismissing a legitimate (if trivial) complaint with 'Get your own fucking Frisbee'
jokes.explanation: Functional gag about rookie cops not matching their own expectations. The 'get your own Frisbee' dismissal is a decent punchline that shows Jenko's laziness and contempt, but the setup is a bit generic.

jokes.text: Jenko spots bikers smoking weed and identifies it as 'Cannabis sativa.' Schmidt: 'Chaka Khan.' Jenko: 'Chaka Khan?'
jokes.setup: Jenko uses the scientific name 'Cannabis sativa' — showing off unexpected knowledge
jokes.punchline: Schmidt fires back with 'Chaka Khan' as if it's a similarly legitimate drug identification term, making no sense whatsoever — and then Jenko earnestly repeating it back as a question suggests he's not sure if he missed something
jokes.explanation: Genuinely odd and funny. Schmidt's random deployment of 'Chaka Khan' as drug terminology is absurdist but lands because of the rhythm — Jenko said something educated, Schmidt matched the cadence with something completely meaningless. Jenko's confused echo sells it. The inexplicability is the joke, and it works.

jokes.text: Bikers' excuses for smoking weed: 'I have glaucoma.' / 'I get nervous in crowds.' / 'Herpes.'
jokes.setup: Jenko confronts the bikers about marijuana use and asks if they've forgotten it's illegal
jokes.punchline: Three escalating non-sequitur justifications — the third, 'Herpes,' doesn't even pretend to be related to marijuana use and the escalation into complete absurdity is the joke
jokes.explanation: Classic rule-of-three with a deliberately absurd third beat. 'Herpes' as a reason for smoking marijuana is funny precisely because it makes no attempt at justification — it's pure non-sequitur escalation. Well-structured, good economy, though the characters delivering it are throwaway.

jokes.text: 'You want me to beat your dick off? ... I'll beat your dick off with both hands. What's up? Let's go.' / 'That's weird, man.'
jokes.setup: Jenko is trying to intimidate a biker with a threat — 'You want me to beat your dick off?'
jokes.punchline: Schmidt's matter-of-fact 'That's weird, man' followed by his polite attempt to interpret what Jenko meant — 'he's going to punch you so many times around the genital area that your dick's just going to fall off' — which is somehow even weirder
jokes.explanation: Two-stage joke that earns its laughs: Jenko's malapropistic threat is funny on its own, but Schmidt's earnest clarification — delivered as if doing Jenko a favor — makes it land harder. Schmidt spelling out the mechanics ('so many times around the genital area') in a helpful, clinical tone is perfect character comedy. The structure is strong: weird line → acknowledgment → worse explanation.

jokes.text: Biker: 'Man, you guys even real cops? You look like the kids on Halloween.' / 'If those boys is cops, I'm DEA.'
jokes.setup: Schmidt and Jenko try to assert authority over the biker gang
jokes.punchline: The bikers mock them as too young/small to be real cops — 'like kids on Halloween' — then the DEA line doubles down with self-undermining sarcasm
jokes.explanation: 'Like kids on Halloween' is a good simile — evocative and specific. The DEA callback is a nice rhythmic button. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Jenko chasing his perp: 'Don't run from me! You're making it worse for yourself!' / 'I'm going to shoot you if you don't slow down, man! Come on!'
jokes.setup: Jenko is chasing a drug dealer on foot — a dramatic cop pursuit
jokes.punchline: His threats are oddly casual and pleading — 'Come on!' reads as a teenager whining rather than a cop commanding, undercutting the action-movie moment
jokes.explanation: Decent character moment — Jenko's cop voice revealing itself as a teenager's voice is consistent comedy. The 'Come on!' at the end of a shooting threat is the best beat. Not particularly original but serves the character and scene.

jokes.text: 'I'm not playing any more! I'm so not kidding!'
jokes.setup: Schmidt is also chasing his perp and trying to sound authoritative
jokes.punchline: 'I'm so not kidding' — Schmidt's attempt at a cop threat comes out as the kind of thing a frustrated child says, perfectly betraying his nerd identity under the cop exterior
jokes.explanation: 'I'm so not kidding' as a cop threat is Schmidt in a nutshell — he wants to be authoritative but his actual personality keeps leaking through. The phrasing is very specific and very funny. Good character economy.

jokes.text: Schmidt wrestling a perp: 'You're a pussy!' — from the perp. Schmidt: 'You got the right to... Give me that! You got the right to—' and then tries to read Miranda rights during the fight
jokes.setup: Schmidt has finally caught his perp and is trying to arrest him properly by reading Miranda rights
jokes.punchline: He attempts to Mirandize someone who is actively fighting him — the juxtaposition of legal formality and physical chaos, plus his Miranda rights being interrupted mid-sentence
jokes.explanation: Good physical-meets-character comedy moment. The idea of trying to recite legal rights during an active fight is a solid bit. It also plants the Miranda callback that pays off later in the episode.

jokes.text: Post-arrest celebration: 'What's up?' / 'Drop my nuts on your motherfucking forehead!' / 'That's right.' / 'Fuck you, park!' / 'We arrest people now!'
jokes.setup: Jenko and Schmidt have made their first arrest and are euphoric
jokes.punchline: Their trash-talking devolves into increasingly unhinged declarations — 'Drop my nuts on your motherfucking forehead' and 'Fuck you, park!' directed at no one in particular — revealing them as immature kids in cop suits
jokes.explanation: 'Fuck you, park!' is the standout line — taunting an inanimate public space captures the childish absurdity of their victory lap. The escalating obscenity of the celebration vs. the mundaneness of a park drug arrest is good comic contrast.

jokes.text: Schmidt tries to claim he read the Miranda rights: 'I did read him his right... I did a version of that.'
jokes.setup: Captain tells them the arrest was dropped because they forgot to read Miranda rights
jokes.punchline: 'I did a version of that' — Schmidt's desperate self-justification implies that his version bore little resemblance to the actual Miranda warning
jokes.explanation: Economic and character-specific. 'A version of that' is a great weasel phrase — it doesn't deny the charge while also not accepting it. Perfect Schmidt hedge. The callback to the fight scene pays off well.

jokes.text: Captain makes Schmidt recite the Miranda rights on the spot. Schmidt: 'Look, it obviously starts with, "You have the right to remain silent."... I think it sounds something like...' long pause.
jokes.setup: Captain challenges Schmidt to recite the four sentences every cop must know. Schmidt confidently starts.
jokes.punchline: He gets through the first line and then clearly blanks — the long trailing 'I think it sounds something like...' followed by nothing is the comedic beat
jokes.explanation: Good sustained cringe. The setup includes Jenko's smug 'We got time' and the captain noting it's only '57 words' — making Schmidt's failure more humiliating. The scene works as a cringe sequence even if no single line is exceptional.

jokes.text: 'You have the right to remain an attorney.' / 'Did you say that you have the right to be an attorney?' / 'You do have the right to be an attorney, if you want to.'
jokes.setup: Schmidt is attempting to recite the Miranda rights from memory and fumbles 'You have the right to an attorney'
jokes.punchline: He accidentally merges 'remain silent' and 'right to an attorney' into 'You have the right to remain an attorney' — a grammatically coherent but legally meaningless sentence — and then doubles down when called out
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in the reel. The malapropism itself is clever — Schmidt genuinely blends the two phrases in a way that sounds plausible mid-recitation. But Jenko's immediate incredulous echo ('Did you say you have the RIGHT to BE an attorney?') and Schmidt's doubling-down ('You DO have the right to be an attorney, if you want to') turn a good malapropism into a three-beat escalating absurdity. It's also a perfect payoff to the Miranda setup. Quotable, specific, and shows both characters clearly.

jokes.text: Captain asks Jenko how the chase went. Jenko: 'Honestly, he did get away, and he threw me down pretty hard. Actually fucked up my elbow pretty bad.'
jokes.setup: Captain asks 'And how did that go for you?' — clearly a rhetorical question meant to emphasize failure
jokes.punchline: Jenko answers with complete honesty and a request for elbow sympathy — not registering that this is a disciplinary context
jokes.explanation: Good Jenko character moment — his obliviousness to social register means he answers a rhetorical humiliation question with a sincere injury report. The 'Can I see that?' / 'Yeah, actually, it hurts cause the dirt gets mushed into it' is a nice button showing the captain indulges him.

jokes.text: 'We're reviving a canceled undercover police program from the '80s and revamping it for modern times. You see, the guys in charge of this stuff lack creativity and are completely out of ideas, so all they do now is recycle shit from the past and expect us all not to notice.'
jokes.setup: Captain is explaining the Jump Street undercover program to the two new recruits
jokes.punchline: He's transparently describing the film's own premise — a remake/reboot — and directly acknowledging that the studio is recycling the '80s TV show
jokes.explanation: One of the great meta moments in mainstream comedy films. The joke works on multiple levels: it's funny in the moment as character dialogue, it's a genuine critique of Hollywood reboot culture, and it pre-emptively disarms any criticism of the film itself. The delivery in-character by the Captain (not winking at the camera) makes it land harder. This is comparable to the 8.0 anchor — specific, quotable, surprising, and efficiently executed. It earns the 8+ score.

jokes.text: Schmidt asks if they're being sent to a 'child sex slavery ring.' Jenko: 'Sir, if I have to suck somebody's dick, I will. It's just... I'd prefer not to.'
jokes.setup: Captain describes the undercover program as requiring 'immature-seeming' young officers. Schmidt wildly misinterprets this.
jokes.punchline: Jenko's volunteering to perform sexual acts as part of undercover duty — with the qualifier 'I'd prefer not to' — is a spectacularly misplaced statement of professional dedication
jokes.explanation: The 'I'd prefer not to' Bartleby reference is probably unintentional but the phrasing is exquisitely polite for the content. Jenko treating sexual acts as an unfortunate but acceptable professional obligation — delivered with complete sincerity — is very funny. The escalation from Schmidt's absurd interpretation to Jenko's even more absurd response works well.

jokes.text: Schmidt's response to the undercover program: 'Sir, are you saying that you're going to send us into, like, a child sex slavery ring or something?'
jokes.setup: Captain mentions they need 'young, immature-seeming officers' for a program
jokes.punchline: Schmidt's mind goes immediately to the worst possible interpretation — child sex slavery ring — which is both wildly off-base and somewhat character-revealing
jokes.explanation: Funny because the leap from 'undercover program' to 'child sex slavery ring' is so extreme. Schmidt's anxiety and catastrophizing tendencies make this character-consistent.

jokes.text: Captain: 'Down on Jump Street.' / 'Is it... 37 Jump Street?' / 'No, that doesn't sound right.'
jokes.setup: Captain tells them to report to Jump Street and gives the address
jokes.punchline: One of them mishears or adjusts the address to '37 Jump Street' — a nod to the film sequel '22 Jump Street' — before correcting to the right number, playing with the franchise's self-awareness
jokes.explanation: Minor meta joke playing with the title number. Gets a small laugh on first watch, slightly more on rewatch when you've seen the sequel. Not especially sophisticated but the self-awareness is consistent with the film's comedic mode.

jokes.text: Jenko and Schmidt arrive at 21 Jump Street to find it's housed in a church. 'Aroma of Christ Church?'
jokes.setup: They've been told to report to an elite undercover unit — built up as impressive
jokes.punchline: The deflation of arriving at a rundown church, with Schmidt reading the apparently real sign: 'Aroma of Christ Church' — a genuinely funny church name that undercuts all dramatic buildup
jokes.explanation: 'Aroma of Christ Church' as a church name is funny on its own — it sounds like a real but unfortunate name. The reveal that this is their impressive new posting deflates expectations efficiently. Visual gag dependent on the production design.

jokes.text: Sign on the church reads 'Aroma of Christ Church' — Schmidt reads it aloud with a confused pause
jokes.setup: They pull up to what turns out to be their new precinct — a church
jokes.punchline: 'Aroma of Christ Church' — a name that sounds like it describes a smell, implying the church smells like Christ specifically
jokes.explanation: The church name joke is quietly funny — 'Aroma of Christ' is a real type of church name but it's inherently absurd on its face. The confused reading of it is the visual gag. Not a big laugh but a nice texture joke.

jokes.text: Captain Dickson's entrance: 'Everybody comfortable? Yeah.' [pause] 'Get your motherfucking ass up when I'm talking!'
jokes.setup: Captain Dickson asks in a calm, friendly tone if everyone's comfortable. The recruits relax.
jokes.punchline: He immediately explodes into furious profanity — the whiplash from genial to volcanic is the joke
jokes.explanation: Classic false-calm-then-explosion structure, but executed very well by Ice Cube. The calm 'Yeah.' before the explosion gives the audience just enough time to relax. The whiplash timing is what makes this work — it's well-constructed even if the structure is familiar.

jokes.text: Captain Dickson calls Jenko and Schmidt 'Justin Beaver, Miley Cyrus-looking motherfuckers'
jokes.setup: Dickson is explaining why they were chosen — they look young enough to pass as high schoolers
jokes.punchline: His description of their youthful looks via tween pop star comparisons — delivered as an insult — is the joke. 'Justin Beaver' (mispronouncing Bieber) adds a small extra layer.
jokes.explanation: 'Justin Beaver' is a small nice touch — Dickson can't even get the reference right, which suits the character. The Miley Cyrus comparison to Channing Tatum is funny given the physical disparity. Solid if not exceptional.

jokes.text: Dickson: 'You some Justin Beaver, Miley Cyrus-looking motherfuckers.' / Schmidt whispers: 'Captain Sassy.'
jokes.setup: Dickson is explaining why they were chosen — they look young
jokes.punchline: 'Justin Beaver' (not Bieber) + Schmidt's whispered 'Captain Sassy' — two simultaneous jokes layered together
jokes.explanation: 'Justin Beaver' is a small but deliberate mispronunciation (either Dickson doesn't know or doesn't care). 'Captain Sassy' as Schmidt's whispered nickname is a great character beat — Schmidt, terrified, still can't resist nicknaming authority figures. Both jokes work individually and are enhanced by proximity.

jokes.text: Captain Dickson's 'Angry Black Captain' speech: 'I know what you're thinking, "Angry Black Captain." It ain't nothing but a stupid stereotype. Well, guess what, motherfuckers. I'm black. And I worked my ass off to be the captain! And sometimes I get angry. So suck a dick!'
jokes.setup: Dickson preemptively addresses the obvious perception of him as a stereotype
jokes.punchline: He dismantles the stereotype label — then immediately confirms every element of it while insisting it's not a stereotype. 'So suck a dick!' as the triumphant conclusion to a speech about not being an angry stereotype is perfect irony.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel and one of Ice Cube's signature moments. The structure is exceptional: acknowledge stereotype → subvert it → completely embody it while denying it. The self-awareness is genuine rather than cheap because it's rooted in a real character who actually IS those things. 'So suck a dick!' as the concluding argument is an inspired punchline. This earns 8+ — it's specific, quotable, structurally tight, and only works with this character.

jokes.text: Dickson sizing up Jenko and Schmidt: 'Like this guy right here. Handsome. And he's probably a dummy. And then this guy. He's short and insecure. And he's probably good with money.'
jokes.setup: Dickson is demonstrating the concept of 'embracing stereotypes' by applying them to his new recruits
jokes.punchline: He stereotype-profiles Jenko (handsome = dummy) and Schmidt (short = good with money, i.e. Jewish stereotype) matter-of-factly. Schmidt's incredulous 'What the fuck?' reaction sells it.
jokes.explanation: Good extension of the stereotype theme, and accurate to both characters (Jenko IS a dummy, Schmidt IS insecure). Schmidt's 'What the fuck?' reaction to being Jewish-stereotyped by his new captain is funny. The accuracy of the stereotypes makes it smarter than a random insult.

jokes.text: Dickson's Jump Street rules — 'Fugazy' and 'Burns' as rule names, delivered with total authority
jokes.setup: Dickson lays out the rules of Jump Street with ominous gravitas
jokes.punchline: The rules are named 'Fugazy' and 'Burns' — presumably after former officers — giving mundane rules (don't get expelled, don't have sex with students) an absurdly bureaucratic mythology
jokes.explanation: Minor absurdist touch — the rules having proper names implies a whole history of officers who violated them, which is funny backstory worldbuilding. Not a huge laugh but adds texture.

jokes.text: Schmidt volunteering: 'Sir, I know we come off as a couple of lady-killers, but I promise you we will be super professional.' Dickson: 'Clearly, I wasn't talking to you, Big Titties. You cherub-looking motherfucker.'
jokes.setup: Schmidt tries to be reassuring about the 'no sexual relations' rule, implying it's a concern for someone who attracts that kind of attention
jokes.punchline: Dickson cuts him down with 'Big Titties' and 'cherub-looking motherfucker' — the insults are insulting AND accurate, and the implication is that Schmidt is so unattractive the rule doesn't apply to him
jokes.explanation: 'Cherub-looking motherfucker' is a great insult — evocative, specific, and funny because cherubs are inherently ridiculous. 'Big Titties' as a nickname lands because it's both crude and oddly affectionate coming from Dickson. Schmidt's oblivious self-regard walking into this is well-structured.

jokes.text: Billiam Willingham introduces the drug, its street name 'H.F.S.,' and then explains: 'Holy fucking shit.' / 'Holy...' / 'They put this on the Internet for everybody to see?' / 'They're teenagers, man. They're really stupid.'
jokes.setup: Billiam says the drug goes by the street name 'H.F.S.' — sounds like a coded drug name
jokes.punchline: He explains it literally means 'Holy Fucking Shit' — an acronym kids chose for a drug that's just their immediate reaction to it. Dickson's addendum that teenagers are 'really stupid' lands as the topper.
jokes.explanation: The drug acronym revelation is a solid misdirection-to-punchline. The audience expects something coded or scientific; getting 'Holy Fucking Shit' is funny because it's both appropriate (strong drug) and stupid (terrible brand). The beat of characters reacting to it being on the internet adds a nice layer.

jokes.text: Video of the dead kid asking his girlfriend to prom — 'Jessica, will you go to prom with me? But I already know the answer. It's yes.' — playing in the briefing room
jokes.setup: They're watching a video of the kid who overdosed before we know he's dead
jokes.punchline: His confident prom proposal ('I already know the answer. It's yes.') is charming and funny — until they inform us he's dead. The humor comes from the gap between his breezy confidence and the tragic outcome.
jokes.explanation: The humor is bittersweet and dark — the kid's charisma makes us like him, which makes the reveal more affecting and the comedy darker. 'I could watch this kid all day' followed by 'He's dead' is a good dark comedy beat. The prom proposal itself ('I already know the answer. It's yes.') is funny on its own as confident teenager behavior.

jokes.text: Dickson watching teenager drug video: 'I could watch this kid all day. Man, this kid rules. Ruled. His parents found him OD'd in his room a few days ago. He's dead.'
jokes.setup: Dickson is watching an enthusiastic teen doing a drug stunt on video — amused by his antics
jokes.punchline: Mid-sentence, 'Ruled' correcting 'rules' — the pivot from present to past tense a beat before the death reveal. The casualness of 'He's dead.' is the punchline.
jokes.explanation: This is a brilliantly economical dark-comedy moment. The mid-sentence tense correction ('Ruled') does the whole job — the audience hears the past tense and already knows what's coming, but the matter-of-fact 'He's dead.' still lands as a jolt. The sequence of enjoying the video, then correcting tense, then delivering the death news in a single flat sentence is structurally near-perfect. Dickson's voice never changes register. High economy — the entire joke is essentially the word 'Ruled.' in context.

jokes.text: 'And as you can see, this kid is white. That means people actually give a shit.' / 'Sir, I just want to throw out to you that I would give a shit if he was black.'
jokes.setup: Billiam is explaining the urgency of the drug case and why there's political pressure
jokes.punchline: He baldly states that the case gets attention because the victim is white. Schmidt's immediate protest that he personally would give a shit regardless is a perfect earnest-liberal overcorrection that lands as funnier than the original cynical observation.
jokes.explanation: Sharp social commentary delivered as dark comedy. Billiam's blunt statement is funny in its corporate cynicism. But Schmidt's knee-jerk progressive protest — 'I would give a shit if he was black' — is funnier because it's simultaneously sincere, oblivious, and proves Billiam's point about the performativity of these responses. Good writing.

jokes.text: Dickson reveals he enrolled Schmidt in honors chemistry because 'says you were a virgin through high school.' / 'It says that?' / 'No. I just assumed it, due to your many years on the honor roll and your membership to the juggling squad.'
jokes.setup: Dickson is explaining Schmidt's undercover enrollment — he looked at Schmidt's real high school transcript
jokes.punchline: Dickson faked having documentary evidence for his insult, then reveals he just assumed Schmidt was a virgin because of nerd markers — honor roll and juggling. The escalation from 'it says that?' (genuine alarm that his virginity status is documented) to the reveal is well-structured.
jokes.explanation: Layered joke: the fake-out ('it says that?' is Schmidt's horror), the reveal that it's just an assumption, and then the specificity of 'juggling squad' as a nerd-marker. The juggling squad is a perfect detail — it's specific enough to be funny rather than generic. This is tight writing with good character specificity.

jokes.text: "Schmidt, says you were a virgin through high school." / "It says that?" / "No. I just assumed it, due to your many years on the honor roll and your membership to the juggling squad."
jokes.setup: Captain reviews Schmidt's file and delivers what sounds like it was written there
jokes.punchline: He admits he made it up — deduced from the honor roll and juggling squad, which he treats as self-evident proof of virginity
jokes.explanation: The pivot from 'says you were a virgin' to 'No, I just assumed it' is a great structural beat. The specificity of 'juggling squad' as proof of sexual failure is unexpected and character-specific. The escalation from honor roll (plausible) to juggling squad (perfect detail) is well-constructed.

jokes.text: Schmidt: 'It's the Juggling Society, but it's fine. It's fine.'
jokes.setup: Dickson called it the 'juggling squad'
jokes.punchline: Schmidt corrects the name with the dignity of someone defending a legitimate institution — 'The Juggling Society' — then immediately accepts it doesn't matter: 'but it's fine. It's fine.'
jokes.explanation: The doubled 'it's fine' tells us everything — Schmidt is NOT fine with this but is trying to be professional. The correction of 'squad' to 'Society' shows residual pride in an organization that everyone else finds pathetic. Perfect character economy in four words.

jokes.text: Dickson repeating the mission brief: 'Infiltrate the dealers, find the supplier.' / Schmidt: 'But if we find the supplier first...' / 'God damn. Infiltrate the dealers, find the supplier.'
jokes.setup: Dickson gives simple two-step mission instructions. Schmidt tries to optimize them.
jokes.punchline: Schmidt's genuinely logical counter-argument ('if we find the supplier first, we don't have to worry about the dealers') is treated as idiotic insubordination. Dickson's exhausted repetition — now prefaced with 'God damn' — is the punchline.
jokes.explanation: Good bureaucratic comedy — Schmidt's question is actually smart and Dickson's refusal to engage with it makes no logical sense, which is the joke. It also characterizes both men: Schmidt overthinks, Dickson issues orders and expects compliance. The 'God damn' addition to the third repetition shows escalating frustration perfectly.

jokes.text: Schmidt praying to Korean Jesus: 'Hey, Korean Jesus. I don't know if you only cater to Korean Christians or if you even exist. No offense.'
jokes.setup: Schmidt is alone in the Jump Street chapel before the assignment, nervous about going back to high school
jokes.punchline: He addresses the statue as 'Korean Jesus' — a formally dressed Korean Jesus statue in the church — with the agnostic hedge 'I don't know if you even exist. No offense.' The politeness of the disclaimer is what sells it.
jokes.explanation: 'No offense' appended to 'I don't know if you even exist' is a perfect Schmidt move — covering his bases with politeness while being potentially theologically rude. The character-specific nervousness making him pray to a culturally specific statue he found in a repurposed church is well-observed. Korean Jesus becomes a recurring element.

jokes.text: Schmidt praying to "Korean Jesus" — a statue in the Jump Street church — uncertain if he only serves Korean Christians
jokes.setup: Schmidt is alone in the church, apparently anxious about the assignment
jokes.punchline: He prays to a Korean Jesus statue, acknowledging uncertainty about its religious jurisdiction: 'I don't know if you only cater to Korean Christians or if you even exist. No offense.'
jokes.explanation: The Korean Jesus prayer is a genuinely original comedic construction. Schmidt's theological uncertainty about whether a Korean Jesus statue handles general petitions or only Korean ones is a novel, specific, and character-consistent idea. 'No offense' as a hedge to a deity is a perfect economy beat. The prayer itself — anxious, sincere, confused — is a great character moment that blends comedy with genuine vulnerability.

jokes.text: Schmidt ends the prayer: 'Korean Jesus, I just really don't want to fuck this up. I'm sorry for swearing so much. The end? I don't really know how to end a prayer. The end? Yeah.'
jokes.setup: Schmidt has been praying, sincerely expressing his fears
jokes.punchline: He doesn't know how to conclude a prayer — 'The end?' is his attempt, delivered with genuine uncertainty, then confirmed with 'Yeah.' — the casual ending to a religious conversation is both funny and strangely touching
jokes.explanation: The 'The end?' as a prayer closing is exactly what a nerdy, non-religious person would say when they'd run out of things to pray about. The doubling ('The end? ... Yeah.') of self-confirmation is perfect Schmidt voice — anxious, polite, trying his best. High character integration score justified.

jokes.text: Dickson bursts in on the prayer: 'Hey! Stop fucking with Korean Jesus! He ain't got time for your problems. He busy! With Korean shit.'
jokes.setup: Schmidt is having a sincere, private prayer moment
jokes.punchline: Dickson interrupts to protect Korean Jesus's schedule — 'He busy! With Korean shit.' — the specificity of Korean Jesus having a full divine portfolio of exclusively Korean concerns is absurdly funny
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. 'He busy! With Korean shit.' is an exceptional line — the broken grammar ('He busy!') followed by the vague but categorical 'Korean shit' is perfect. It treats Korean Jesus as a real, working deity with a specific and finite jurisdiction. Dickson's protective attitude toward Korean Jesus is funnier than the prayer itself was. Very quotable, high rewatch value. Earns 8+ comfortably.

jokes.text: Schmidt's mom greets him: 'My baby's home! Come here. You will always be my infant angel baby child.'
jokes.setup: Schmidt and Jenko arrive at Schmidt's parents' house for the undercover assignment
jokes.punchline: His mother's greeting escalates through four synonyms for 'baby' — 'infant angel baby child' — each one more infantilizing than the last, while Schmidt clearly wishes he were anywhere else
jokes.explanation: 'Infant angel baby child' is a lovingly absurd escalation. Each word on its own is a reasonable term of endearment; combined they form a weirdly clinical classification. Schmidt's mortification in front of Jenko makes it land harder.

jokes.text: Jenko immediately ingratiating himself with Schmidt's parents: 'Hey! Schmidt family! Up top, Papa Schmidt.' / 'Oh, my God. Mama Schmidt, did you do all this yourself? This is unbelievable. So are you.'
jokes.setup: Jenko, who bullied Schmidt in high school, is now being dropped off at his parents' house
jokes.punchline: He immediately becomes an eager, charming house guest — complimenting the decor and flirting with Schmidt's mom. 'So are you' is a smooth if slightly inappropriate compliment to his friend's mother.
jokes.explanation: Jenko's social ease contrasting with Schmidt's mortification is good character-contrast comedy. 'So are you' to the mom is a small nice touch — Jenko operates on automatic charm even when inappropriate. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Jenko compliments Schmidt's mom: 'Oh, my God. Mama Schmidt, did you do all this yourself? This is unbelievable. It's gorgeous! So are you.'
jokes.setup: Jenko meets Schmidt's parents for the first time
jokes.punchline: 'So are you' — Jenko complimenting Schmidt's mom on her appearance, with the casual ease of someone who flirts reflexively with everyone
jokes.explanation: Good character beat for Jenko — the charm is automatic and inappropriate (this is his partner's mom). Sets up future complications while being funny in the moment.

jokes.text: Schmidt's parents reveal they converted his room into an exercise area: 'We did blow up the air mattress in your room 'cause we're kind of using that as a workout area, so I hope you don't mind the elliptical.'
jokes.setup: Schmidt is returning home as an adult — a dignified professional on a police mission
jokes.punchline: His parents have commandeered his room for their elliptical, relegating him to an air mattress — the universal parental move on adult children that completely deflates his dignity
jokes.explanation: Recognizable and funny but fairly familiar comedy territory. The 'your old room is now a gym' joke is a staple of adult-child-returns-home comedy. Executed well but not especially original.

jokes.text: Schmidt's mom reveals his bedroom now has an elliptical machine because they're using it as a workout area, so he'll be sleeping on an air mattress
jokes.setup: Schmidt is coming home expecting his old bedroom to be there for him
jokes.punchline: His room has been converted to a gym — his parents have moved on so thoroughly they replaced his bed with exercise equipment
jokes.explanation: Solid but familiar 'parents converted your room' joke. Gets a mild laugh. The visual of Jenko touching a Sedona souvenir ('Don't touch that. We just brought it back from Sedona') adds a nice layer.

jokes.text: Schmidt's parents have a memorial wall of his childhood photos and achievements. Schmidt: 'I look like Fred Savage from The Wonder Years, but completely naked, wearing Indian friendship bracelets.'
jokes.setup: Schmidt's parents proudly display his childhood photos, refusing to take them down
jokes.punchline: Schmidt's specific, horrified description of one photo — the precision of 'Fred Savage from The Wonder Years, but completely naked, wearing Indian friendship bracelets' — is funnier than any generic childhood photo embarrassment
jokes.explanation: The specificity of this description is what makes it exceptional — 'Fred Savage, but completely naked, wearing Indian friendship bracelets' paints a very specific and very funny mental image. Each element escalates the indignity. Schmidt's ability to describe his own humiliation in such vivid detail is a character note (he's the kind of person who over-analyzes his own embarrassments).

jokes.text: Schmidt's dad: 'You look like a young Jay Leno.' — said as a compliment
jokes.setup: Schmidt has described the photo as looking like Fred Savage
jokes.punchline: His dad offers a correction/compliment: 'You look like a young Jay Leno' — Jay Leno being notably less handsome than Fred Savage, delivered as an upgrade
jokes.explanation: The joke works because Schmidt's dad intends it as a kind correction ('not Fred Savage — Jay Leno!') without recognizing that this is not an improvement. Jay Leno being the affectionate point of comparison for a dad is very specific and funny.

jokes.text: Schmidt's dad: 'You look like a young Jay Leno.' Schmidt: 'Am I even wearing underwear in this picture?' / 'No.'
jokes.setup: Dad is complimenting the childhood photo
jokes.punchline: Schmidt's escalating horror culminates in discovering he wasn't wearing underwear in this widely-displayed family photo. The flat 'No' confirmation from his dad is deadpan perfection.
jokes.explanation: The monosyllabic 'No' from dad — delivered with zero embarrassment — is perfect. It escalates the childhood photo bit naturally: first the visual description (naked-ish), then confirmation he was fully naked, then dad completely unbothered by this. The 'Jay Leno' insult-compliment is also good — it's what a dad would sincerely mean as praise.

jokes.text: Schmidt: 'Am I even wearing underwear in this picture?' / Beat / Dad: 'No.' / Schmidt: 'I remember. You know why? Because I've told it to a therapist about 8,000 times.'
jokes.setup: Schmidt looks at a childhood photo and questions whether he's wearing underwear
jokes.punchline: He confirms he's not, then reveals he's processed this specific nude-childhood-photo-trauma in therapy 8,000 times
jokes.explanation: The '8,000 times in therapy' detail is excellent — it's both a number absurd enough to be funny and specific enough to feel real. The beat before 'No' (the dad knowing exactly what photo and immediately confirming he's naked) is good structural timing. Establishes Schmidt's psychological backstory economically and darkly.

jokes.text: Schmidt: 'Because I've told it to a therapist about 8,000 times.'
jokes.setup: Dad starts to explain why he remembers details about the naked photo
jokes.punchline: Schmidt preemptively finishes the story — revealing he has processed this specific memory approximately 8,000 times in therapy
jokes.explanation: Good economy — '8,000 times' as the number of therapy sessions implies a whole sad history of Schmidt working through his childhood humiliations. The specificity of the exaggerated number is funnier than a vague 'many times.' Consistent character work.

jokes.text: Schmidt identifies a trophy as 'a fourth grade participation medal for soccer. It's literally a medal for sucking.' Dad: 'No, that is a medal for trying.'
jokes.setup: Schmidt's parents have proudly displayed all his childhood achievements including participation trophies
jokes.punchline: Schmidt cuts through the parental euphemism: 'It's literally a medal for sucking.' Dad's earnest correction — 'That is a medal for trying' — is funnier than Schmidt's cynicism because Dad genuinely believes it.
jokes.explanation: The participation trophy bit is fairly common observational comedy territory, but 'a medal for sucking' is a sharp articulation of it. Dad's sincere reframe — 'a medal for trying' — adds a layer: Dad isn't stupid, he just genuinely values effort, which is both touching and funny.

jokes.text: Schmidt realizes his mom has told the neighbor Phyllis about his undercover assignment: 'Mom, you told Phyllis I was here? She's going to tell the whole neighborhood.' Mom: 'Undercover. That's so cute.'
jokes.setup: Schmidt has emphasized that his assignment is 'super secretive'
jokes.punchline: His mom has already blown his cover with the neighbor, and dismisses his concerns with 'That's so cute' — treating his police work as an adorable hobby rather than serious law enforcement
jokes.explanation: 'That's so cute' as a response to legitimate police concerns is perfectly condescending in the way only a mother can be. Functional character comedy that reinforces Schmidt's domestically humiliating situation.

jokes.text: Schmidt studying their fake identities: 'Forget those identities. They're bullshit. They said I was held back a year.' Jenko: 'You were. You were held back two years.' / 'Just 'cause it's a fake backstory doesn't mean it doesn't hurt my feelings.'
jokes.setup: Schmidt complains that his fake undercover identity is insulting
jokes.punchline: Jenko reveals the insult is accurate — he was held back — then Schmidt's response acknowledges the fictional/real blur: 'doesn't mean it doesn't hurt my feelings.' He's upset about a true thing being in his fake backstory.
jokes.explanation: Very good joke structure: the revelation (it's true) and Schmidt's perfectly illogical response (it still hurts even though it's true because it was presented as a fiction). The gap between 'fake backstory' and 'my feelings' is excellent character logic — Schmidt is simultaneously self-aware and completely unable to compartmentalize.

jokes.text: Jenko obsessing over his outfit on the first day: 'Fuck! Socks don't match. I got to start all over. It's the first day of school, dude. I got to look awesome.'
jokes.setup: These are adult cops who have been through the police academy and made their first arrest
jokes.punchline: Jenko regresses immediately to full high-schooler anxiety about his outfit — 'I got to look awesome' delivered with dead seriousness
jokes.explanation: Good character note — Jenko mentally never left high school, so going back causes genuine first-day anxiety. His regression is consistent and funny, even if the specific joke is not very elaborate.

jokes.text: Schmidt: 'You know, back in the day, you were super popular, and I wasn't as much... You don't think that's going to happen again, do you?' Jenko: 'No. Come on, man. We're adults now. We're best buds. It's definitely not going to happen again.'
jokes.setup: Schmidt articulates the obvious dramatic irony: Jenko was the popular bully, Schmidt the unpopular nerd. Will history repeat?
jokes.punchline: Jenko's emphatic reassurance 'It's definitely not going to happen again. We're good.' — delivered with complete sincerity — is funny because the audience knows absolutely it will happen again. The 'definitely' doing maximum ironic work.
jokes.explanation: Dramatic irony played straightforwardly. The audience knows this will absolutely happen. Jenko's sincerity makes it land — he genuinely believes himself. Not original but executed competently, and sets up plot expectations.

jokes.text: Schmidt: 'You know, back in the day, you were super popular, and I wasn't as much. We didn't really get along in high school. You don't think that's going to happen again, do you?' / Jenko: 'No. Come on, man. We're adults now. We're best buds. It's definitely not going to happen again.'
jokes.setup: Schmidt raises the anxiety that their old high school dynamic might reassert itself
jokes.punchline: Jenko's very confident 'It's definitely not going to happen again' — which the audience knows is dramatic irony foreshadowing that it absolutely will happen again
jokes.explanation: Classic dramatic irony setup — Jenko's certainty ('definitely not') reads as a promise to the audience that it will happen, and it's funny because the film has established exactly why it will. Rewatch bonus because on second viewing you know immediately what's coming.

jokes.text: Schmidt's dad cheerfully says good morning. Jenko snaps: 'Just shut up.'
jokes.setup: Schmidt's dad greets them on their first-day-of-school morning with 'Beautiful day out there, boys.'
jokes.punchline: Jenko, clearly full of first-day anxiety, tells the man good-naturedly 'Just shut up' — revealing his morning-of nerves
jokes.explanation: Quick character beat. Jenko's snapping at the innocent dad is good — it shows he's nervous despite his bravado. The dad presumably takes no offense, which makes Jenko's rudeness funnier.

jokes.text: Schmidt practices Miranda rights in the car: '...You have the right to an attorney. If you cannot afford an attorney, one will be appointed...' Jenko: 'Dude, do you still not know the Miranda rights? You're a cop.' Schmidt: 'Come on, man. They always cut away on TV before they finish them.'
jokes.setup: Schmidt is still not confident in his Miranda rights after the earlier incident
jokes.punchline: His excuse — 'they always cut away on TV before they finish them' — is both meta (they ARE in a movie) and a genuinely plausible reason a cop-show-raised person might not know them. The TV-taught cop is a perfect absurd logic.
jokes.explanation: Excellent payoff to the Miranda running gag. 'They always cut away on TV before they finish them' is a great meta joke that also reveals something true about how cop shows actually work. It's funny as a character justification and funnier as a meta-commentary. This is the best beat in the Miranda thread.

jokes.text: Jenko delivers 'The Three Keys of Coolness in High School' — a list that goes to five items — and includes 'be handsome' as #3
jokes.setup: Jenko positions himself as the expert on high school coolness and begins an authoritative list
jokes.punchline: The list keeps expanding past three ('Four, if anyone steps to you on the first day...') and includes 'be handsome' as a genuine tip — advice that only helps if you already have it, completely useless as instruction
jokes.explanation: The list exceeding its own stated count is a good structural joke. 'Be handsome' as genuine advice is perfect Jenko — he genuinely doesn't understand why this isn't helpful because he has always been handsome. The complete sincerity makes it land. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Jenko's coolness advice includes: 'Two, make fun of people who do try.' He looks directly at Schmidt as he says this.
jokes.setup: Jenko is giving Schmidt genuinely the advice he followed in high school
jokes.punchline: Rule #2 is to mock people who try hard — looking at Schmidt, who is literally trying hard to absorb these rules
jokes.explanation: Decent visual/character beat — the implied look at Schmidt makes this more than just a list item. It's both advice and a subtle insult directed at the person he's advising.

jokes.text: They arrive at school and immediately discover their 'kick-ass car' is a sensible, boring vehicle. 'Shit.' [as the car is revealed to be disappointing]
jokes.setup: Rule 5 of Jenko's coolness list: 'Drive a kick-ass car'
jokes.punchline: Their actual assigned car is emphatically not kick-ass — 'Shit.' immediately undercuts rule 5
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural callback — Rule 5 is immediately violated by reality. The single word 'Shit.' as the entire response is good economy. The visual gag depends entirely on the car reveal working, which it presumably does.

jokes.text: Police captain hands them the keys and says 'just don't be driving it like teenagers, revving up the engine and shit.' / 'We would never.' / 'Come on, Hoffs. Give us a little credit.'
jokes.setup: Hoffs warns them not to drive recklessly — a reasonable caution for two immature cops
jokes.punchline: Schmidt's indignant 'We would never' and Jenko's 'Give us a little credit' — immediately before they absolutely do drive like teenagers
jokes.explanation: Classic dramatic irony setup — their emphatic denial of what they're about to do is the joke. Well-structured even if the execution is predictable.

jokes.text: They drive the car off a ramp or do something dramatic with it, then emerge ecstatic: 'That was awesome! That was amazing. Was I flying?' Jenko: 'That was amazing. All right, do mine, do mine.'
jokes.setup: The irony setup is paid off — they immediately drive like teenagers
jokes.punchline: Their genuine, childlike wonder — 'Was I flying?' — reveals they did something physically reckless and loved it. 'Do mine, do mine' shows they're taking turns, like kids with a new toy.
jokes.explanation: The payoff works — 'Was I flying?' is a genuinely funny line in context. The image of two grown cops taking turns doing something recklessly stupid with their government-issued vehicle is consistent character comedy. 'Do mine, do mine' has an endearing childish quality.

jokes.text: After Jenko's turn: 'You okay?' / 'I think I shit my pants.'
jokes.setup: Jenko does whatever reckless driving stunt they were doing
jokes.punchline: 'I think I shit my pants' — delivered with genuine uncertainty about whether this happened — is both scatological and perfectly timed. The 'I think' qualifier (he's not sure) makes it funnier than certainty would.
jokes.explanation: Four words, maximum laugh. 'I think I shit my pants' works because (1) the 'I think' — he's genuinely checking — is funnier than certainty, (2) it confirms the stunt was actually terrifying despite their bravado, and (3) it ends the sequence perfectly. Pure economy.

jokes.text: Arriving at school, Jenko says: 'Hey, park in that handicapped spot. It'll make us look cool.' Schmidt: 'That's awesome.'
jokes.setup: They're arriving at their first undercover day at school and strategizing about appearing cool
jokes.punchline: Jenko's theory that parking in a handicapped spot reads as cool rather than illegal and inconsiderate — and Schmidt's immediate enthusiastic agreement — perfectly encapsulates their adolescent regression and poor judgment
jokes.explanation: Good ending beat for the reel. The idea that handicapped parking reads as an alpha move is a funny high school logic that actual teenagers might believe. Schmidt's instant, unquestioning 'That's awesome' shows how completely Jenko has already reasserted dominance over him — the dynamic reversal predicted at 20:26 is already happening.

jokes.text: Jenko and Schmidt debate one-strap vs. two-strap backpacks while approaching a high school, with Jenko caving to peer pressure mid-stride
jokes.setup: Schmidt insists one-strap is the way to go; Jenko starts caving immediately upon seeing other students
jokes.punchline: 'Don't succumb to the peer pressure.' — said by the cop who is immediately succumbing to peer pressure
jokes.explanation: Works well because it immediately characterizes Jenko as someone who desperately wants to fit in, undercutting his own advice in real time. Character-specific and efficiently delivered.

jokes.text: Schmidt looks at an unidentifiable student clique and says 'What the fuck are those things? I'm so confused right now.'
jokes.setup: The two cops are trying to read the social landscape of the modern high school
jokes.punchline: Schmidt cannot categorize a clique at all — suggesting how much high school culture has changed since they were students
jokes.explanation: Functional observational gag about generational confusion; economical but not particularly fresh.

jokes.text: Eric's biodiesel car 'smells like egg rolls' — runs on leftover fry oil from Hunan Palace
jokes.setup: Eric brags about his eco-friendly biodiesel car
jokes.punchline: Jenko: 'Smells like egg rolls.' Eric confirms it runs on Hunan Palace fry oil — the mundane specificity undercuts the environmental smugness
jokes.explanation: The specific restaurant name ('Hunan Palace') elevates this above a generic eco-joke. The deflation of green smugness via fast-food grease is a solid comedic concept, efficiently executed.

jokes.text: Jenko's response to environmental concern: 'Whatever, man. I don't care about anything.'
jokes.setup: Eric lectures about global crisis and riding bikes
jokes.punchline: Jenko's posturing non-answer: total nihilist detachment as a cool-kid affectation
jokes.explanation: Quick character beat — Jenko trying on the 'cool detachment' persona. Works because it's exactly the wrong thing to say to eco-kids, and he doesn't realize it.

jokes.text: Jenko punches a kid for playing 'gay-ass music,' the kid turns out to be gay, and Jenko tries to retroactively justify it
jokes.setup: Jenko tells a studying kid to turn off his 'gay-ass music' and punches him
jokes.punchline: 'I didn't punch him because he's gay. I punched him, and then he happened to turn out to be gay afterwards.'
jokes.explanation: The escalation is well-structured: casual slur → surprise reveal → panicked non-apology. The logic Jenko uses ('he happened to turn out to be gay afterwards') is a funny bit of motivated reasoning. The film is clearly satirizing this attitude rather than endorsing it.

jokes.text: 'In a weird way, it might have been homophobic NOT to punch you just because you were gay.'
jokes.setup: Jenko is trying to defend punching a gay kid and failing; Schmidt attempts to help
jokes.punchline: Schmidt's tortured reverse-logic defense: not punching someone because they're gay is itself discriminatory
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in this reel. The inverted equality-logic is a genuinely clever piece of absurdist reasoning — it sounds almost like a real argument, which makes it funnier. It's well-structured, quotable, and the student's 'Right' agreement makes it land even harder. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor; earns its score.

jokes.text: Principal Dadier: 'You punched a little gay black kid in the face, and it's not even second period.'
jokes.setup: Dadier is dressing down Jenko and Schmidt in his office
jokes.punchline: The specificity of 'not even second period' reframes the depravity as a time-management problem
jokes.explanation: The time-of-day qualifier turns a disciplinary statement into dark comedy. Very economical and the deadpan delivery implied by the principal's character makes it land. Genuinely funny line.

jokes.text: Dadier: 'I am one more black gay kid getting punched in the face away from a nervous breakdown.'
jokes.setup: Dadier is laying out why the school is a mess and why he's at his limit
jokes.punchline: He quantifies his breakdown threshold with hyper-specific criteria — exactly one more punched gay kid
jokes.explanation: Extends the callback effectively. The quantification ('one more') is funny because it implies this has happened before. Good character establishment for Dadier as someone barely holding it together.

jokes.text: Dadier assigns identities — 'Which one of you is Doug?' — then has to repeat it because they're being weird
jokes.setup: After the whole punishment speech, Dadier moves to business
jokes.punchline: 'Let's do that again and pretend you guys aren't weird.'
jokes.explanation: Mild but functional. Dadier's weary re-do request is a good beat for his character. The awkward pause that prompts it carries the laugh.

jokes.text: Jenko and Schmidt accidentally swap identities — Jenko (the dumb one) is assigned to AP Chemistry; Schmidt (the smart one) gets Drama
jokes.setup: Dadier pegs Schmidt as 'brainy type' and Jenko as 'drama geek' based on looks
jokes.punchline: He has them exactly backwards — the smart one is in drama, the dumb one is in AP Chem
jokes.explanation: Smart structural move — sets up a running problem that will pay off throughout the film. The irony of Schmidt ending up in drama while the dumb jock gets science is well-integrated into character dynamics. Dadier's 'I wouldn't have taken you for the brainy type' earns a laugh on its own.

jokes.text: Schmidt panics: 'I'm in drama. I suck at drama. It's girly and embarrassing.'
jokes.setup: They've received the wrong class assignments
jokes.punchline: Schmidt's hilariously outdated attitude toward drama — the precise opposite of current cool-kid culture
jokes.explanation: Works as character comedy — Schmidt's reflexive dismissal of drama as 'girly' shows how out of touch he is with the new high school culture. Functional but not especially sharp.

jokes.text: Jenko: 'I can fake my way through band practice and app chemistry for a few weeks.' Schmidt: 'AP Chemistry. AP Chemistry. And, no, you can't, because you don't even know what it's actually fucking called!'
jokes.setup: Jenko confidently claims he can handle Schmidt's hard classes
jokes.punchline: He calls AP Chemistry 'app chemistry' — the correction becomes the proof of his incompetence
jokes.explanation: Elegant self-proving joke. Jenko's confidence is immediately demolished by the evidence embedded in his own speech. Schmidt's frustrated repetition and the meta-point ('you don't even know what it's called!') is perfectly economical. Strong structure.

jokes.text: Jenko: 'Chemistry's the one with the shapes and shit, right?' Schmidt: 'Fuck.'
jokes.setup: Schmidt insists Jenko can't fake AP Chemistry
jokes.punchline: Jenko thinks chemistry is 'the one with the shapes' — confusing it with geometry; Schmidt's single-word 'Fuck.' is the punchline
jokes.explanation: One of the tightest jokes in the reel. The 'shapes and shit' is a hilariously confident wrong answer (he's describing geometry or maybe molecular diagrams but clearly has no idea), and Schmidt's single devastated 'Fuck.' is the perfect button. Maximum economy — nine words total carry a full comedic arc.

jokes.text: Drama teacher mid-anecdote about booking a TV commercial in Albany, completely ignoring the students
jokes.setup: The drama teacher is supposed to be addressing the class about the dead student
jokes.punchline: He's rambling about his own career in Albany, completely self-absorbed
jokes.explanation: Stock 'narcissistic drama teacher' archetype. Gets a mild smile but doesn't do anything especially new with the type.

jokes.text: Schmidt to Molly: 'So are you saying if he wasn't talented, it would be less sad?' — then immediately: 'I was just busting your balls.'
jokes.setup: Molly says 'It's really sad about that kid. He was talented.' — a sincere grief moment
jokes.punchline: Schmidt immediately interrogates the logic, then tries to salvage it with 'just busting your balls' — doubly awkward because it's a girl
jokes.explanation: Good cringe beat — Schmidt's social awkwardness in a situation that calls for empathy, compounded by using a masculine idiom on a girl. Shows his desperation to seem casual. The recovery attempt is as bad as the original gaffe.

jokes.text: Drama teacher: 'I remember, one time, doing cocaine with Willie Nelson's horse, and we were having so much fun. And then I realized that she was dead.'
jokes.setup: Teacher is rambling through increasingly inappropriate anecdotes about his past
jokes.punchline: The story pivots from charming drug-fueled memory to 'then I realized she was dead' — delivered as casual reminiscence
jokes.explanation: Genuinely surprising and dark. The structure is excellent: 'Willie Nelson's horse' is already absurd, the cocaine detail escalates it, and 'she was dead' lands as a complete tonal left-turn delivered with utter equanimity. Quotable, memorable, and specific enough to feel fresh rather than randomly weird. Earns its high score.

jokes.text: Drama teacher: 'Drugs are bad. But they can have their place in the life of a professional actor. Notice the distinction. I said professional actor.'
jokes.setup: Teacher awkwardly walks back his drug talk to teenagers after a drug-related death
jokes.punchline: His disclaimer — 'professional actor' — is the thinnest possible hedge, delivered as though it resolves everything
jokes.explanation: Good button on the drama teacher's drug riff. The repeated emphasis on 'professional actor' as a magical qualifier is funny and character-specific. The delivery-of-disclaimer format works well.

jokes.text: 'New person. Mr. Texty Texty... You look like you might have a little Peter inside of you.'
jokes.setup: Teacher singles out Schmidt (texting) to audition for Peter Pan
jokes.punchline: 'You might have a little Peter inside of you' — unintentional double entendre
jokes.explanation: Classic unintentional double entendre. Gets a laugh but is pretty much the most obvious joke available given 'Peter Pan.' Not particularly clever but well-timed.

jokes.text: Drama teacher: 'Doug, you never won't know what you can't achieve before you don't achieve it.'
jokes.setup: Schmidt tries to get out of auditioning
jokes.punchline: The teacher delivers a motivational speech that is grammatically/logically a complete tangle of negatives
jokes.explanation: Smart wordplay — the quadruple negative sounds inspirational but means nothing (or possibly the opposite of inspiration). Good character comedy for the clueless drama teacher who thinks this is profound. Original and economical.

jokes.text: AP Chemistry student raps a poem about water molecules: 'My favorite molecule is water / I'd marry it, unless it was my daughter'
jokes.setup: 'Molecule Mondays' — students share creative science content
jokes.punchline: The rap is earnestly terrible: the rhyme scheme works but 'unless it was my daughter' is a deeply weird line, delivered with total commitment
jokes.explanation: The 'unless it was my daughter' line is what makes this memorable — it starts as quirky nerd content and then goes somewhere genuinely strange. The commitment to the bit sells it. Good absurdist character work.

jokes.text: Water rap continues: 'It allowed life to form on ancient Mars, and we use it to wash our cars. H2O. H2O. H2O.'
jokes.setup: Continuation of the molecule rap
jokes.punchline: The bathos of pivoting from 'ancient Mars' to 'wash our cars' — the rhyme forces an absurd juxtaposition
jokes.explanation: Continuation of the previous joke; the diminishing-grandeur rhyme (Mars → cars) is funny but slightly weaker than the daughter line.

jokes.text: AP Chemistry teacher: 'Okay. Time for a pop Quiznos.' Student: 'A what?' Teacher: 'It's a quiz, and the first person who finishes gets a $10 gift certificate to Quiznos.'
jokes.setup: Teacher announces a 'pop Quiznos'
jokes.punchline: It's literally a 'pop quiz' rebranded with Quiznos sponsorship — the mundane real-world explanation is the joke
jokes.explanation: Clever and economical — the portmanteau works, the reveal is funny ('the first person who finishes gets a $10 gift certificate'), and it's a good satirical jab at corporate sponsorship creep. Tight construction.

jokes.text: Student to Jenko: 'You look really old. Were you held back or something?' Jenko: 'No. You look super young. Were you held forward?'
jokes.setup: Student points out Jenko looks too old for high school
jokes.punchline: Jenko's comeback 'were you held forward?' — a meaningless but symmetrical reversal
jokes.explanation: 'Were you held forward?' is a great line — it sounds like a real comeback but is semantically absurd (you can't be 'held forward'). Jenko delivers it with complete confidence. High quotability and excellent economy.

jokes.text: Jenko's cover story for his age: 'I went to school in France, so they do, like, two extra years of middle school there. It's so lame.'
jokes.setup: Student presses Jenko on why he looks so old
jokes.punchline: The fabricated French school system excuse, delivered with casual teenage irritation ('It's so lame')
jokes.explanation: The 'It's so lame' is a nice touch — Jenko commits to the persona even in the cover story. Functional character humor.

jokes.text: AP Chem teacher: 'French, the language of love.' — then gives Jenko a lingering look
jokes.setup: Jenko mentions going to school in France
jokes.punchline: Teacher's non-sequitur romantic aside followed by an uncomfortable gaze at Jenko
jokes.explanation: Mild cringe beat — the teacher's inappropriate attention toward Jenko is a running undercurrent. Gets a mild laugh but doesn't develop into much here.

jokes.text: Schmidt attempts to audition for Peter Pan and completely botches 'I've gotta crow' — the drama teacher gives notes: 'Maybe try one cooler. And faster. And louder. And better. And less insecure and more just cool.'
jokes.setup: Schmidt has been forced to audition despite having no drama experience
jokes.punchline: The cascading list of notes — each one more contradictory and unhelpful — is funnier than any single bad audition
jokes.explanation: The escalating list of useless notes ('one cooler... less insecure and more just cool') is good comedy writing — each note sounds vaguely helpful but adds up to nothing actionable. The final 'less insecure and more just cool' is the best note.

jokes.text: Schmidt: 'I'm going to run outside, and I'm going to utilize those, and I'm going to come back.' — then sprints out the door
jokes.setup: Schmidt has received a pile of useless director's notes
jokes.punchline: He treats the bad notes with absolute earnest sincerity, actually runs outside to 'utilize' them
jokes.explanation: Good character beat — Schmidt's earnestness is funny here. The physical commitment (actually running out) elevates it beyond just a line reading.

jokes.text: AP Chem teacher, flustered after looking at Jenko's chest: 'Not like that. Just, let me check you out. Let me check out your chest. Check out your test... Let me... Let me grade your quiz.'
jokes.setup: Teacher is trying to grade Jenko's test but is visibly attracted to him
jokes.punchline: She fumbles through increasingly suspicious word-substitutions in real time
jokes.explanation: The verbal self-correction chain (chest → test → quiz) is well-constructed — each step of the cover-up is worse than the previous. Good cringe escalation and character specificity.

jokes.text: Jenko: 'Can I go take a dump?' Teacher: 'Yeah, okay. That's cool. We have this hurry back rule, so if you're not back in six minutes, I have to send you to the principal... I guess this will have to be a quickie.'
jokes.setup: Jenko asks to leave class to go to the bathroom
jokes.punchline: 'I guess this will have to be a quickie' — said about the bathroom trip, but clearly functioning as a double entendre given her attraction to him
jokes.explanation: Another inadvertent double entendre from the teacher. Functional, gets a laugh, but slightly repetitive with the previous cringe beat.

jokes.text: Jenko and Schmidt approach the drug dealer (the yearbook kid) nervously; Schmidt asks 'So do you make the stuff or...' Dealer: 'Do I look like a fucking scientist? No, I just sell it.'
jokes.setup: Schmidt tries to seem casual while buying drugs from the yearbook kid
jokes.punchline: The dealer's irritated 'Do I look like a fucking scientist?' — the mundane offended professionalism of a small-time dealer
jokes.explanation: Good beat — the dealer's irritation at being confused with a producer is a nice character moment. The 'fucking scientist' indignation is funny.

jokes.text: Dealer asks 'You guys aren't narcs, are you?' — Schmidt immediately yells 'WHOA!' and accuses the dealer of being a narc: 'You know who calls people narcs? Narcs, narc.'
jokes.setup: The dealer reasonably asks if they're cops
jokes.punchline: Schmidt's panicked over-denial using circular logic ('narcs call people narcs, so if you call us narcs, you're the narc') — which immediately collapses
jokes.explanation: Smart joke — the circular logic sounds almost plausible for a split second before it collapses. Schmidt's desperate over-reaction is perfect character comedy, and the film is self-aware about undercover cop clichés. Genuinely funny and quotable.

jokes.text: Schmidt tries to explain his circular narc logic to the dealer: 'Because if you call us narcs, if narcs call people narcs, and you call us narcs, then that's kind of...'
jokes.setup: Schmidt doubles down on explaining his narc logic
jokes.punchline: The explanation just trails off into nothing because even Schmidt can hear it falling apart
jokes.explanation: Extension of the previous joke. The trailing-off is a good beat but slightly weaker than the initial delivery of the logic.

jokes.text: Schmidt: 'I was going to take it, and then masturbate later.'
jokes.setup: Dealer tells them to take the drugs there; Jenko and Schmidt explain they were going to take them home
jokes.punchline: Schmidt overshares his entire plan, including the post-drug masturbation
jokes.explanation: Perfect TMI character moment for Schmidt — his genuine, honest description of his plan crosses a line without meaning to. The overshare is so specific it becomes endearing and funny. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Jenko, after swallowing the pill: 'I love doing drugs at school.' Schmidt: 'I'll just take the drugs right here, in our mouths.'
jokes.setup: They've been forced to take the drugs on the spot
jokes.punchline: Both try to narrate their own compliance as if it's a reasonable and chosen activity; the phrasing 'in our mouths' is hilariously over-literal
jokes.explanation: The 'in our mouths' specification is unnecessary and therefore funny — Schmidt narrating the obvious as though providing helpful clarification. Good beat.

jokes.text: Jenko: 'What is that? Barbecue? Cool Ranch?'
jokes.setup: Jenko has just swallowed an unknown drug pill
jokes.punchline: He evaluates it like a chip flavor rather than a drug
jokes.explanation: Very economical — two chip flavor names do a lot of work. The incongruity of treating a drug like a Dorito is sharp and character-specific for Jenko.

jokes.text: They try to make themselves throw up — Schmidt suggests: 'Your grandma's vagina, and there's a dick going into it.'
jokes.setup: They realize they've taken a drug that killed a kid and need to vomit
jokes.punchline: Schmidt's attempt at a gross-out image is aggressively specific and extremely wrong for the situation
jokes.explanation: The specificity of Schmidt's gross-out attempt — particularly directing it at Jenko's grandmother — is the joke. His frantic 'I don't know! I'm just trying!' sells it. Good panic energy.

jokes.text: Jenko: 'Dude, let's just finger each other's mouths.' / Schmidt: 'No!' / Jenko: 'Do you wanna die? Do you wanna die?'
jokes.setup: Attempts to self-induce vomiting are failing
jokes.punchline: Jenko's solution — mutual mouth-fingering — sounds horrifying as a thing two straight male friends would do, but is proposed with total pragmatic sincerity; 'Do you wanna die?' as the survival argument
jokes.explanation: Good cringe comedy. The logic is sound (it IS how you induce vomiting) but the social discomfort between two straight guys makes it funny. 'Do you wanna die?' as the clinching argument is well-delivered.

jokes.text: Jenko: 'Dude, let's just finger each other's mouths.' Schmidt: 'No!' ... 'Do you wanna die? Do you wanna die?' — escalating to them actually doing it in the school hallway
jokes.setup: They can't make themselves vomit any other way
jokes.punchline: The mutual finger-in-mouth vomit attempt, happening in a school hallway, with Schmidt screaming 'Just stick it in!'
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'we have to throw up' to 'finger each other's mouths' in a school hallway is well-paced, and the dialogue ('Just stick it in!', 'Cut your fucking fingernails!') layers on the cringe. The physical comedy reads strongly even from dialogue alone.

jokes.text: While Jenko fingers Schmidt's mouth to induce vomiting, Schmidt moans: 'What are you doing? Are you trying to find my G-spot?'
jokes.setup: Jenko is trying to trigger Schmidt's gag reflex by putting his fingers in Schmidt's mouth
jokes.punchline: Schmidt's involuntary comparison of the uncomfortable experience to G-spot seeking — which both undermines his own heterosexuality and captures the absurdity of the moment
jokes.explanation: Good extension of the cringe sequence. 'G-spot' as the wrong anatomical reference is funny — it's the wrong body part from the wrong sexual context, which makes it weirder and funnier than if he'd made the obvious joke.

jokes.text: Schmidt: 'Cut your fucking fingernails!'
jokes.setup: Jenko is trying to finger Schmidt's throat in the hallway
jokes.punchline: The practical complaint about fingernail length in the middle of this absurd emergency
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy — five words that land perfectly because the mundane hygiene complaint is so incongruous with the life-or-death situation. One of the better one-liners in the reel.

jokes.text: Security guard stops Jenko and Schmidt running in the halls, compliments Jenko's muscle tone: 'When'd you go through puberty? Like, at seven or something? You look like you're in your mid-20s, for crying out loud.'
jokes.setup: They're running through the halls post-finger-vomit attempt and get stopped by a guard
jokes.punchline: The guard notices Jenko looks absurdly old for a high schooler while simultaneously being distracted by his physique
jokes.explanation: Returns to the 'Jenko looks too old' joke from chemistry class. The 'at seven or something' line is good but the bit is starting to show repetition.

jokes.text: Guard, while yelling at Jenko, suddenly sees Jenko raise his hand to gesture and treats it as a physical threat: 'What the hell was that? Don't ever raise your hand to me like that again. I consider that a threat.'
jokes.setup: Jenko is trying to explain who he is
jokes.punchline: Guard's hair-trigger intimidation response to a completely innocent gesture — his paranoia/tough-guy act is overblown
jokes.explanation: Good character beat for the guard. The hair-trigger 'I consider that a threat' response to a hand gesture is funny in its overblown machismo.

jokes.text: Guard describes his track team: 'My track team is full of physically incapable rejects. I mean, if I wasn't the coach, I'd be laughing my ass off at how spastic they are, but I am the coach, so I need you.'
jokes.setup: Guard/coach needs Jenko to run for his team
jokes.punchline: He describes his own team with brutal contempt, then pivots to needing them — the casual self-awareness of his team's awfulness
jokes.explanation: Good character-specific humor — the coach's complete honesty about his team is funny because coaches typically don't admit this. 'If I wasn't the coach, I'd be laughing my ass off' is a good line.

jokes.text: Guard/coach tells Jenko to sign the hall pass deal: 'Don't blow on me, son.'
jokes.setup: Jenko is wavering on agreeing to run anchor at the track meet
jokes.punchline: 'Don't blow on me, son' — a weirdly intimate and idiosyncratic way to say 'don't let me down'
jokes.explanation: Very good character-specific phrase — 'blow on me' instead of 'let me down' is an oddly physical idiom that feels native to this specific character. High economy, memorable.

jokes.text: Guard/coach looks at the two of them and says 'Are you guys on drugs?'
jokes.setup: Jenko and Schmidt are clearly acting strangely from the pill they took
jokes.punchline: The guard asks the one question that is literally true while they're trying to cover it up — but the guard has no idea
jokes.explanation: Classic dramatic irony beat — the audience knows the answer is yes. Functional but not particularly fresh as a comedic device.

jokes.text: Coach reacts to something Schmidt/Jenko does with his tongue: 'I don't like that. Put your tongue back in your mouth. Put your tongue in your mouth, and close it. What are you doing? Stop it. Actually, that's not bad.'
jokes.setup: The coach is in the middle of a transaction / agreement with the guys
jokes.punchline: His series of objections culminates in a reluctant admission that whatever the tongue thing is — it's 'not bad.' The reversal of his emphatic disgust into mild approval is the joke.
