jokes.explanation: Funny sequence. The repeated prohibitions followed by a capitulation works as escalation with a reversal. The fact that we don't know exactly what the tongue gesture IS adds to the absurdist quality.

jokes.text: Jenko in AP Chemistry, high and panicking: 'One particle of Unobtainium has a nuclear reaction with a flux capacitor. Carry the two, changing its atomic isotoner into a radioactive spider. Fuck you, science!'
jokes.setup: Jenko is taking a chemistry quiz while high
jokes.punchline: His answer is a mash of sci-fi movie references (Avatar, Back to the Future, Spider-Man) delivered as confident chemistry, culminating in 'Fuck you, science!'
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. The pop-culture science mashup (Unobtainium + flux capacitor + radioactive spider) is genuinely clever — each element is from a different beloved franchise, and together they form a coherent-sounding fake chemistry sentence. 'Fuck you, science!' as the concluding punctuation is perfect. High quotability, strong character integration (only Jenko would know exactly these sci-fi properties and nothing else). Comparable to the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: Schmidt, high, nails the Peter Pan audition and sings 'I've gotta crow' with full commitment — the drama class reacts with awe
jokes.setup: Schmidt has been trying to avoid the audition; he's now high on an unknown drug
jokes.punchline: The drug makes him perform spectacularly — the thing he was most afraid of becomes his best moment, and the class treats it as a revelation
jokes.explanation: Strong payoff to the earlier failed audition. The irony of the drug enabling peak performance is a good structural joke, and 'Welcome aboard, Peter' as the button is perfectly timed.

jokes.text: Track coach cheering Jenko at the meet: 'Huge lead! We got this!' — then Jenko runs the wrong way, throws the baton, and the coach devolves into 'Run that way! Spike that! Fuck you, Miles Davis!'
jokes.setup: Jenko, high, is running anchor leg of the relay
jokes.punchline: He runs the wrong way, throws the baton, and the coach's commentary deteriorates into 'Fuck you, Miles Davis!' — a completely inexplicable non-sequitur
jokes.explanation: The escalation from excitement to chaos to 'Fuck you, Miles Davis!' is excellently structured. The Miles Davis non-sequitur is what elevates this — it's not 'Fuck you!' but specifically Miles Davis, which is inexplicable and therefore hilarious. High quotability and rewatch value. Strong physical comedy inferred from the dialogue.

jokes.text: Coach, holding the stray baton: 'That is a baton penis.' — after Jenko has apparently done something suggestive with the baton
jokes.setup: Jenko has thrown/handled the baton in a way that looks phallic during his drug episode
jokes.punchline: The coach's flat, matter-of-fact anatomical identification of what he's witnessing — not horrified, just naming it
jokes.explanation: Four words, maximum economy. The clinical categorization 'baton penis' as the coach's entire response to what he's witnessing is very funny. The deadpan delivery makes it land harder than any elaboration would.

jokes.text: Eric reframes Jenko's disastrous track race as intentional sabotage: 'That was awesome how you sabotaged that track meet, man. Organized sports are so fascist.'
jokes.setup: Jenko has just humiliated himself and his team in the relay
jokes.punchline: Eric interprets the drug-fueled disaster as a principled anti-establishment statement
jokes.explanation: Perfect character-based irony. Eric's interpretation says everything about his worldview — his progressive frame turns any bizarre behavior into political statement. 'Organized sports are so fascist' is a great line and highly quotable. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Jenko: 'That's just what I do.' — accepting the false credit
jokes.setup: Eric praises Jenko for 'sabotaging' the race
jokes.punchline: Jenko immediately and smoothly takes credit for the drug accident as intentional political action
jokes.explanation: Four words, maximum efficiency. Jenko's instant pivot to owning the disaster is good character comedy. Works as a button on the previous joke.

jokes.text: Captain Dickson: 'Who put this together? Are you autistic?' Jenko: 'It is artistic, sir, because the thing is, the yarn actually indicates...'
jokes.setup: Jenko proudly presents the board; Captain insults it
jokes.punchline: Jenko misreads 'autistic' as 'artistic' and takes it as a compliment — defending the board on artistic merit
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback joke. Jenko's misreading 'autistic' as 'artistic' is both funny and character-specific — it confirms his enormous blind spot about his own intelligence while also showing his genuine pride in the board. The misread is subtle enough to require the audience to do a small amount of work, which pays off.

jokes.text: Captain reads the board: 'Lead dealer, Eric Molson. Alpha dog. Sick chicks, killer steeze. Did the AIDS run this year. He's getting into Berkeley, early admish, and he totally gets me.'
jokes.setup: The investigators are supposed to be building a drug case; Schmidt has compiled a profile of Eric
jokes.punchline: The profile reads as a crush/fan letter — 'he totally gets me' as the final point reveals Schmidt has become enamored with the target
jokes.explanation: Very funny character moment. 'He totally gets me' as a law enforcement profile note is a perfect reveal of Schmidt's subconscious priorities. The escalation from actual intel to personal connection ('and he totally gets me') is well-structured. 'Killer steeze' and 'early admish' are fun vernacular choices.

jokes.text: Captain: 'We just brought down a group of wannabe thugs stripping down cars in the Garfield High metal shop. Meanwhile, you two were standing around finger-popping each other's assholes.'
jokes.setup: Captain compares his successful operation with Jenko and Schmidt's slow progress
jokes.punchline: 'Finger-popping each other's assholes' as a descriptor for their ineffective investigation — also an accidental callback to the literal fingering scene
jokes.explanation: Works on two levels: as generic slang for incompetence AND as an accidental callback to what they were literally doing in the hallway earlier. Dickson's character voice is consistent and vivid. High quotability.

jokes.text: Schmidt tries to infiltrate the chemistry classroom — arrives to find nerds playing Bakugan with a password-protected door
jokes.setup: Schmidt announces he's about to infiltrate a 'super high-tech drug manufacturing ring in the chemistry classroom'
jokes.punchline: The 'ring' is just nerds with a card game and a comically excessive password door — the deflation of his confidence
jokes.explanation: Good structural payoff — Schmidt's big declaration is immediately deflated by the mundane reality. The password-protected door followed by Bakugan is a solid visual setup/payoff.

jokes.text: 'Ms. Griggs gave us one so we could work, tutor, deal Bakugan.' — the accidental parallel of 'deal Bakugan' to drug dealing
jokes.setup: Schmidt asks how they got a key to the chemistry room
jokes.punchline: 'Deal Bakugan' — the word 'deal' in the context of the drug investigation creates an inadvertent double meaning
jokes.explanation: Economical joke — 'deal Bakugan' does double duty. Works better in context because Schmidt just left a speech about infiltrating a drug ring.

jokes.text: Schmidt asks the nerd what a covalent bond is to test him; the nerd correctly answers, then says 'I know everything.' Schmidt: 'Okay.' — a perfectly flat non-response
jokes.setup: Schmidt tries to establish academic superiority over the nerd
jokes.punchline: The nerd knows exactly what a covalent bond is AND declares omniscience; Schmidt's 'Okay.' is a defeated acceptance
jokes.explanation: Good deadpan beat — Schmidt's one-word 'Okay.' in response to 'I know everything' is perfectly economical. The nerd's confident omniscience claim paired with Schmidt's total surrender is funny.

jokes.text: Nerd: 'No, I can't install a spyware to remotely monitor calls or anything that the mic picks up. I can't do that at all.' — obviously he can
jokes.setup: Schmidt asks if the nerd can listen in on phone calls
jokes.punchline: The nerd's overly specific denial ('I can't do that at all') is a textbook 'I cannot confirm this' — which immediately confirms it
jokes.explanation: Smart joke — the specificity of what he 'can't' do is exactly how you'd phrase it if you could. Jenko and Schmidt's reactions ('Is he being sarcastic?' / 'So you can.') work as a good tag. Well-structured.

jokes.text: Schmidt laments to Jenko: 'Liking comic books is popular. Environmental awareness, being tolerant. If I was just born 10 years later, I would have been the coolest person ever.' Jenko: 'I know. It's bullshit.'
jokes.setup: Schmidt observes the new high school social order
jokes.punchline: His realization that his actual personality — nerdy, tolerant, earnest — would have been cool if he'd been born in the right decade
jokes.explanation: One of the most thematically rich jokes in the reel. It articulates the film's central premise (high school social order has inverted) through personal character revelation. Schmidt's genuine grievance is funny and relatable. Jenko's 'I know. It's bullshit.' is a perfect agreement from the wrong side of this observation. High character integration.

jokes.text: Schmidt: 'You know what? I totally know the cause. Glee. Fuck you, Glee.'
jokes.setup: They're trying to understand why nerd culture became cool
jokes.punchline: Schmidt identifies Glee as the culprit with disproportionate personal outrage
jokes.explanation: Very economical and quotable. 'Fuck you, Glee' is exactly the right amount of petty outrage directed at the right cultural target — it's specific, funny, and reveals character. High quotability. The directness of the insult lands well.

jokes.text: It's Doug Schmug McQuaid. / It's so weird that you're calling me. I pretty much text except for when a random old relative calls.
jokes.setup: Schmidt calls Molly on the phone, an action that feels normal to him
jokes.punchline: Molly treats a phone call like something only an old relative would do, implying Schmidt is ancient for calling instead of texting
jokes.explanation: Sharp generational joke that efficiently establishes the age-gap comedy the film is built on. Schmidt's undercover persona is immediately undermined by the most mundane social norm. Good economy, solid character work.

jokes.text: Mom, get off the phone! / I love you, honey, Dougie, Doug, Douglas McQuaid. / Mom, so serious right now! Stop!
jokes.setup: Schmidt is trying to have a cool teenage conversation with Molly
jokes.punchline: His mom gets on the line, smothers him with affection, and uses his full undercover alias which sounds absurd said aloud three ways
jokes.explanation: Classic embarrassing-parent interruption, elevated by the specificity of the name 'Dougie, Doug, Douglas McQuaid' which makes the undercover alias sound ridiculous. The cringe is earned but the structure is familiar.

jokes.text: I'm sorry. My mom's such a dick. She just, like, smothers me with affection and makes me feel like I'm five years old.
jokes.setup: Schmidt apologizes for his mom being embarrassing
jokes.punchline: He calls her 'a dick' for the crime of loving him too much — the inversion of what 'dick' behavior usually means
jokes.explanation: The contradiction of calling an affectionate mom 'a dick' is a clean ironic inversion. It also foreshadows Schmidt's deeper insecurities about maturity. Good character integration for a quick line.

jokes.text: The doctor thought I was gonna spontaneously grow a vagina. I didn't, though, just to be clear.
jokes.setup: Schmidt overshares about his mom buying him 43 stuffed animals, framing it as embarrassingly soft/feminine behavior
jokes.punchline: He escalates to a doctor literally worrying about spontaneous vagina growth — an absurd medical diagnosis — then anxiously clarifies it didn't happen
jokes.explanation: The absurdist medical escalation is unexpected and specific enough to be funny on its own. The anxious clarification ('I didn't, though, just to be clear') is the real punchline — Schmidt so earnest about reassuring Molly he's male makes it land harder.

jokes.text: Yeah, because you already had one. / Exactly. I already had one. / And you don't need two vaginae. You just don't. / Although you could use one as a coin purse.
jokes.setup: Schmidt clarifies he didn't grow a vagina
jokes.punchline: Molly fires back that he already had one (implying he's soft); Schmidt agrees, then they both riff on the coin purse utility of a second vagina
jokes.explanation: The riff escalates beautifully: Molly's comeback, Schmidt's delighted self-agreement, the shared logic of 'you don't need two vaginae,' and the absurd coin purse pivot. Each beat earns the next. The word 'vaginae' (correct Latin plural) in this context is a small gem of comedy economy. Earns rewatch bonus for how naturally the riff flows between two characters.

jokes.text: My dad gave me a stuffed puppy the day he bailed on us. / [beat] / I'm just fucking with you. That is a weird joke.
jokes.setup: Molly says she never got stuffed animals, then 'corrects' herself — her dad gave her one the day he abandoned the family
jokes.punchline: She immediately reveals she was joking, then Schmidt calls it 'a weird joke' — before Molly clarifies her dad DID walk out, just without leaving the puppy
jokes.explanation: Triple-layered joke: (1) dark backstory drop played for laughs, (2) the 'just fucking with you' subversion, (3) the reveal that the dark truth is real anyway — dad DID bail, just without the puppy. 'Just broken dreams' is a nicely ironic kicker. The structure has genuine craft: it tricks the audience twice in quick succession.

jokes.text: No, he did walk out on us, though. But he didn't even leave me a stuffed puppy. Just broken dreams.
jokes.setup: Schmidt asks if her dad really abandoned the family, and Molly confirms it
jokes.punchline: 'Just broken dreams' — delivered flatly as the kicker after the admission, using the stuffed puppy as a comedic contrast to genuine emotional abandonment
jokes.explanation: Economy score is high because 'just broken dreams' does enormous tonal work in three words. The flatness of delivery makes the darkness land as dark comedy rather than pathos.

jokes.text: No, it's just, you know, I don't like when guys are mean to girls. / [Schmidt clearly getting choked up over Molly's story]
jokes.setup: Molly asks if Schmidt is getting choked up after her dad abandonment story
jokes.punchline: Schmidt deflects with a surprisingly sensitive non-sequitur about not liking when guys are mean to girls — revealing he's genuinely emotionally affected while trying to seem tough
jokes.explanation: Character integration is the strength here — Schmidt's earnest sensitivity is completely at odds with the cool undercover persona he's supposed to be projecting. It's funny because it's specific to who Schmidt is as a character, and the deflection is endearing rather than calculating.

jokes.text: Normal transition here. / Actually, I'm having a party next weekend. You should come!
jokes.setup: An awkward emotional moment on the phone after Schmidt gets choked up
jokes.punchline: Molly literally announces 'Normal transition here' before pivoting to party invite — breaking the fourth wall of conversational structure
jokes.explanation: Genuinely clever meta moment — a teenager verbally narrating the awkward conversation pivot she's making is both very real (teens are weirdly self-aware like this) and also a sharp piece of writing that acknowledges the scene's own mechanics. Economy score high because those three words do so much work.

jokes.text: If any of my officers are caught giving alcohol to minors, they'll find theyself in prison with a snorkel duct-taped to they mouth and me shitting down that snorkel.
jokes.setup: Captain Dickson warns Schmidt and Jenko against giving alcohol to minors at their party
jokes.punchline: The threat escalates to an extraordinarily specific, grotesque image of snorkel-based fecal punishment — delivered with complete seriousness
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the film. The specificity is what elevates it — not just a threat, but duct tape, a snorkel, and defecation, delivered as a matter-of-fact warning from an authority figure. 'They'll find theyself' and 'they mouth' (non-standard grammar used consistently) makes it feel authentic to the character rather than a writer's invention. Ice Cube's Captain Dickson is defined by exactly this kind of baroque, escalating profanity. Comparable to an 8+ anchor: unexpected, quotable, specific.

jokes.text: That's extremely vivid. Thank you. / You're the best. You are the best. / Oh, my God. / We love you.
jokes.setup: Captain Dickson just threatened to defecate down a snorkel into their mouths
jokes.punchline: Instead of fear, Schmidt and Jenko respond with sincere gratitude and affection, treating the captain like a beloved mentor
jokes.explanation: The inversion works well: the expected response to a grotesque threat is treated as a touching motivational speech. 'That's extremely vivid. Thank you.' is a perfect deadpan response that's both literal and absurd simultaneously.

jokes.text: "We love you"? What are you doing? Why you saying "I love you" to my mom?
jokes.setup: Schmidt and Jenko have been staying at Jenko's mom's house; Schmidt says 'we love you' on departure
jokes.punchline: Jenko objects to Schmidt's brotherly affection toward his mom as weird — but he just told a superior officer 'we love you' seconds ago without issue
jokes.explanation: Decent character beat — Jenko's selective objection to Schmidt's warmth. Slightly undercut because the funnier version of this joke was already played in id 13. Functional.

jokes.text: How are we going to get drugs for the party? / We got a pound of coke. / We're trying to show them a good time, not ruin their fucking lives. / Pound of marijuana? / Best party ever. / Boo-yah!
jokes.setup: They need drugs for the party but have no connections
jokes.punchline: They immediately produce a pound of cocaine from evidence — Schmidt rejects it on moral grounds, then happily accepts marijuana as the ethical alternative
jokes.explanation: The joke is in Schmidt's precise moral calibration: cocaine = wrong, marijuana = fine, 'best party ever.' The speed of the exchange and the sudden jubilation ('Boo-yah!') after the ethical line is drawn gives it good comic rhythm. The cops-using-evidence-drugs setup is well-established action comedy territory but executed cleanly.

jokes.text: Where is Eric, man? He said he'd be here. / Do we have enough chips? / Is this playlist too dance-y? / Feels too dance-y. / Too dance-y? / What are you talking about? / I don't know, it just feels dance-y.
jokes.setup: The party is barely started and Schmidt and Jenko are anxiously hosting
jokes.punchline: In the middle of a party-crisis about their drug target not showing, Schmidt spirals into existential concern about whether the playlist is 'too dance-y' — a completely trivial hosting anxiety
jokes.explanation: Schmidt's anxious neurosis about playlist vibe while ostensibly on a drug investigation is a solid character beat. 'Dance-y' repeated four times creates a good comic loop. Not exceptional but functional character comedy.

jokes.text: Hey, Paul Blart: Molly Cop. / Such a bad joke. Terrible, terrible.
jokes.setup: Jenko makes a pun combining the film 'Paul Blart: Mall Cop' with Molly's name as she arrives
jokes.punchline: Schmidt immediately and emphatically judges it as a terrible joke — meta-commentary on the quality of the pun from within the film
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: Jenko's pun is genuinely bad (which is the first laugh), and Schmidt's immediate brutal self-aware critique is the real punchline. The film critiquing its own joke from within is a sharp meta move. Rewatch bonus because on second viewing you appreciate how deliberate the bad pun is.

jokes.text: Get ready, get ready, there's Eric. Wait for the signal. And then you come in here looking like a rock-solid 10.
jokes.setup: Schmidt coaches Jenko before Eric arrives, treating their undercover party infiltration like a sports play
jokes.punchline: The pep-talk language ('rock-solid 10') is completely self-unaware — Schmidt hyping Jenko's social attractiveness as a tactical asset
jokes.explanation: Functional setup moment, mild laugh from Schmidt's tactical seriousness in a social situation. Nothing exceptional — the joke is mostly in Schmidt's earnestness, which is recurring character work rather than a specifically crafted gag.

jokes.text: Eco Suave. / Whoa. / Wow, so I'm really digging this decor. Very Native American. / Yeah, our parents are actually really into Native American... / Let's rock and roll.
jokes.setup: Eric arrives at the party and immediately comments on the decor
jokes.punchline: Eric's 'Eco Suave' persona leads him to compliment 'Very Native American' decor — an oblivious, vaguely appropriative remark — while simultaneously cutting off Schmidt's explanation to get to the drugs
jokes.explanation: Eric's character is well-established through this — the eco-hippie bro who does a weed deal with the same energy as a lifestyle compliment. 'Very Native American' is a good specific detail for a lazy appropriator. 'Let's rock and roll' cutting off the explanation is the punchline.

jokes.text: Come on, CSI the shit out of this thing.
jokes.setup: Jenko and Schmidt are frantically trying to extract data from Eric's SIM card at the party
jokes.punchline: Jenko reduces forensic investigation to a pop-culture verb — 'CSI the shit out of it' — with complete confidence
jokes.explanation: Decent pop-culture reference used as a verb — works because it's Jenko oversimplifying forensics into a TV trope, which is in character. Modest laugh, nothing special.

jokes.text: What the fuck, bro? Some privacy! / Shit, shit, shit! / And that is a really gross three-way. / But what was the girl in the back doing?
jokes.setup: Schmidt bursts into the parents' bedroom to hide with the SIM card reader
jokes.punchline: He interrupts a three-way in progress; Jenko's immediate response is not disgust but curious anatomical inquiry about the girl in the back
jokes.explanation: The pivot from disgust to genuine sexual curiosity is a solid Jenko character beat. 'What was the girl in the back doing?' is a funny deflection that reveals more about Jenko than about the situation.

jokes.text: Read this. 'Please wait. Extracting data from SIM card.' / Shit! It's a bust.
jokes.setup: Jenko urgently demands to know if the SIM card data is ready before Eric leaves
jokes.punchline: Schmidt reads the most mundane software progress bar message as though it's a catastrophic mission failure report
jokes.explanation: Good comic structure: the buildup of urgency ('it's now or never!') deflated by the mundane loading bar message. 'It's a bust' as a police term applied to a software loading screen is a clean juxtaposition.

jokes.text: Keep it casual. / Yeah. / Go with the flow, dude. / Cool, man. / I don't like to make plans or whatever. / You got it.
jokes.setup: After the SIM card bust, they need to stall Eric without looking desperate
jokes.punchline: Their coaching each other to 'keep it casual' becomes so intense and choreographed that it becomes the opposite of casual — a nervous theatrical performance of casualness
jokes.explanation: Solid irony: trying so hard to seem casual that the effort itself becomes visible. Works because Jonah Hill and Channing Tatum's physical performances would amplify this. Functional comedy moment.

jokes.text: Hey, why you here, Scott? What, Kennedy High isn't having any parties tonight?
jokes.setup: A rival drug dealer named Scott shows up uninvited to the party
jokes.punchline: Eric's challenge is delivered with such condescending cool — the specific detail of naming Kennedy High suggests established territory rivalry, delivered like a don dismissing an interloper
jokes.explanation: Modest setup-establishing beat. Eric's cool-villain energy is consistent. Not a big laugh but efficient character work.

jokes.text: Hey, big player, I don't know who you are. / Don't worry about who I am. / I'm worried about it. / Why? / 'Cause you're at my party right now, dude. This is my temple, this is where I come to find peace, dawg, and you're coming in here like an emotional bull in a china shop, metaphorically knocking over vases, messing with my crew, and I'm like, 'What, Scott, what, Scott, what, what, what, what, Scott?'
jokes.setup: Schmidt steps in to defuse a confrontation between Eric and Scott, trying to seem cool and authoritative
jokes.punchline: His 'intimidating' speech spirals from 'temple of peace' to 'emotional bull in a china shop' to a bizarrely repetitive 'What, Scott, what, Scott' — increasingly unhinged while maintaining complete earnestness
jokes.explanation: One of the funnier Schmidt speeches in the film. The character integration is excellent: Schmidt desperately trying to sound like a cool teen mediator, mixing pseudo-spiritual language ('my temple, my peace') with bro-speak ('dawg'), building to the completely unhinged repetition 'what, Scott, what, Scott.' Jonah Hill's delivery of this kind of controlled-chaos rambling is a signature skill. The 'metaphorically knocking over vases' callback to the actual vase anxiety earlier is a nice structural touch.

jokes.text: It's that kind of party? / Yeah, dude. / Matter of fact, it's getting hot in here, huh? / No, it's getting real. / It's getting very real. / Yeah. It's like seven strangers living in one house. True story. / You want Real World? / Yeah, let's do it, man.
jokes.setup: Confrontation is escalating; Schmidt tries to call Scott's bluff with reality TV metaphors
jokes.punchline: The 'Real World' (MTV show) reference — using it as both a threat and a cultural shorthand for confrontation — is so outdated and odd as a threat that it's funny, then Scott actually accepts the challenge
jokes.explanation: Using MTV's 'The Real World' as fight escalation rhetoric is both dated and funny. The 'seven strangers living in one house' callback to the show's tagline is a good specific detail. Moderate laugh.

jokes.text: It's that kind of party? / Yeah, dude. / Matter of fact, it's getting hot in here, huh? / No, it's getting real. / It's getting very real. / Yeah. It's like seven strangers living in one house. True story. / You want Real World? / Yeah, let's do it, man. / Come on. What's your Real...
jokes.setup: Confrontation is building; Schmidt and Scott trade pop-culture escalation references ('getting hot in here,' Real World)
jokes.punchline: The fight prelude devolves into a bizarre reality TV riff — 'seven strangers living in one house, true story' — before the actual punch
jokes.explanation: Smart comedic choice to have the confrontation escalate through TV-reference posturing rather than actual threats. 'True story' is a great beat — it's the Real World tagline verbatim, used as a genuine threat. The structure builds nicely to the punch. Character-consistent for Schmidt who can't help being pop-culturally verbose.

jokes.text: Schmidt. Doug. / What do I do? / Hit him! / Shit! That hurt worse than when he hit me!
jokes.setup: Scott punches Schmidt; Jenko coaches Schmidt to fight back
jokes.punchline: Schmidt hits Jenko instead of Scott, and immediately complains that hitting Jenko hurt his own hand more than getting punched did
jokes.explanation: Classic slapstick escalation with a good self-aware twist — Schmidt hitting the wrong person is predictable, but his complaint about how much it hurt his own fist landing on Jenko is a solid specific kicker.

jokes.text: Fight normal. / Yo, I'm serious. / Sorry.
jokes.setup: Schmidt is fighting badly during what should be a tense confrontation
jokes.punchline: 'Fight normal' is an absurdly minimal piece of coaching — the simplest possible instruction that implies Schmidt is fighting so abnormally that 'normal' has to be explicitly requested
jokes.explanation: Economy score near-perfect: 'Fight normal' is two words that imply an entire devastating assessment of Schmidt's fighting style. The 'Yo, I'm serious' follow-up confirms it's not a stylistic choice — Schmidt is genuinely fighting wrong. Highly quotable precisely because it's so compact. One of the better economy jokes in the reel.

jokes.text: Seriously, use your words, use your words!
jokes.setup: In the middle of a brawl, Schmidt is being attacked
jokes.punchline: Schmidt yells 'use your words' — a phrase parents say to toddlers to stop them from hitting — in the middle of an actual fight, in the wrong direction (telling his attacker to stop fighting)
jokes.explanation: Applying toddler-management parenting language to a street fight is a sharp absurdist inversion. It's also very Schmidt-specific: he's literally trying to de-escalate a fight using preschool techniques. Quick and efficient.

jokes.text: I kicked him in the nuts.
jokes.setup: The fight is chaotic and violent
jokes.punchline: Schmidt's flat, almost clinical self-report — 'I kicked him in the nuts' — delivered as a simple statement of fact in the middle of chaos
jokes.explanation: The deadpan delivery is the entire joke. Three words, maximum efficiency, completely at odds with the energy of the moment. Works better in performance than on paper.

jokes.text: No, watch my mom's shit, man! / You'll knock over my mom's vase! / Fuck your mom's vase! / Fuck this!
jokes.setup: The fight continues to escalate
jokes.punchline: Schmidt's continued anxiety about his mom's Kokopelli vase during a violent fight, culminating in Scott explicitly saying 'Fuck your mom's vase' — the vase gets its own story arc
jokes.explanation: The Kokopelli vase as a running gag through the fight is a strong structural choice — the mundane domestic anxiety persisting through violence is inherently funny. 'Fuck your mom's vase!' is a great escalation beat because Scott is now furious at an inanimate object. Rewatch bonus for the setup payoff.

jokes.text: That's my brother!
jokes.setup: Jenko does something impressive in the fight
jokes.punchline: Schmidt yells 'That's my brother!' with genuine fraternal pride — except they're not brothers, they're undercover cops pretending to be brothers, making the emotional investment both touching and absurd
jokes.explanation: Layered small moment: Schmidt's genuine pride invests in a fiction he created. It's both a character bonding beat and lightly absurd because of the fake-brothers context established earlier.

jokes.text: Oh, shit. / When did I get stabbed? / That's awesome. / Yeah!
jokes.setup: In the aftermath of the fight, Jenko examines himself
jokes.punchline: He discovers he was stabbed without noticing — the casual 'When did I get stabbed?' treats a stabbing as a minor administrative oversight. Schmidt and others respond with 'That's awesome / Yeah!'
jokes.explanation: The casual discovery of a stab wound is a perfect example of Jenko's character — so macho and endorphin-flooded post-fight that being stabbed is a fun detail rather than an emergency. 'When did I get stabbed?' is highly quotable. The crowd's enthusiastic reaction ('That's awesome / Yeah!') adds to the absurdity.

jokes.text: Is that a cop? / Where? / No, it's not. Here. / I'm so glad we're going back to get my phone. / I just hope we don't wake up Schmidty. / Oh, my God, he's a policeman now. It's like we're living with a narc. / The boy is an angel.
jokes.setup: Molly's friends are discussing Schmidt after the party
jokes.punchline: They joke that Schmidt is 'a narc' and 'a policeman now' — which is literally true, but said as hyperbole about how uncool he is. 'The boy is an angel' is delivered as a fond, oblivious conclusion.
jokes.explanation: Classic dramatic irony: the audience knows Schmidt IS a cop/narc, so characters unknowingly calling him one is a great ironic payoff. 'The boy is an angel' as the punchline underlines the irony — he's simultaneously a narc AND getting glowing reviews for his sweetness.

jokes.text: Pull it out! Pull it out! Pull it out! / Sorry!
jokes.setup: Jenko was stabbed and Schmidt is apparently removing the weapon
jokes.punchline: The repeated 'Pull it out!' chant followed by a meek 'Sorry!' implies whatever came out hurt — the double entendre context and Schmidt's apologetic tone play on the absurdity of field-surgery enthusiasm
jokes.explanation: Modest physical comedy moment. The 'Sorry!' is the best beat. Not particularly inventive but serves as a physical comedy punctuation to the stab wound bit.

jokes.text: That's like us fucking Mother Earth without a condom.
jokes.setup: Someone does something environmentally wasteful at or after the party
jokes.punchline: Eric's eco-warrior persona generates a sexual metaphor for environmental damage — 'fucking Mother Earth without a condom' — delivered with sincere conviction
jokes.explanation: Excellent character-specific line. Only Eric — the teen eco-drug-dealer — could deliver this with straight-faced conviction. The metaphor is both vivid and absurd: environmental concern expressed through unprotected sex imagery. Character integration is very high because this is completely Eric's voice and no one else's. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Get out of my house. I said get out! The party's over! / I'm sorry, Mom, I'm sorry! / The mom is coming! / Let go of me! / You're embarrassing me in front of my friends! / Get back here, you shit!
jokes.setup: The party gets out of hand and Molly's mom returns
jokes.punchline: The mom's escalating fury — culminating in 'Get back here, you shit!' to her own daughter — mirrors Schmidt's earlier description of his mom being 'such a dick' for being too loving, but inverted: this mom is genuinely terrifying
jokes.explanation: Good chaotic energy, 'Get back here, you shit!' is a solid cringe laugh. Fairly standard party-mom-arrives chaos but executed with energy.

jokes.text: You, dude, I like you, man. How do you feel about making a little extra money? / Whatever it is, I'm in.
jokes.setup: Eric approaches Jenko after Jenko distinguished himself in the fight
jokes.punchline: Eric immediately recruits Jenko for drug dealing; Jenko agrees without hearing a single detail — 'Whatever it is, I'm in' — which is both very Jenko and very funny as an undercover cop
jokes.explanation: Jenko's impulsive 'Whatever it is, I'm in' is perfect for his character — enthusiastic, no-questions-asked, completely at odds with cop procedure. Good character-comedy beat that also advances plot.

jokes.text: 'I love dick'? / You think that's funny? / 'Wonder Years douche'? / What kind of a sick animal draws an ejaculating penis into an 8-year-old's mouth?
jokes.setup: Schmidt returns home and his mom has discovered graffiti drawn on Schmidt's childhood room photo or poster
jokes.punchline: The escalating specificity of the graffiti — 'I love dick,' 'Wonder Years douche,' and an 'ejaculating penis into an 8-year-old's mouth' — described with maternal horror by his mom
jokes.explanation: The escalation of graffiti descriptions is well-paced, with 'ejaculating penis into an 8-year-old's mouth' as the horrified peak. The mom delivering this with outraged specificity is funnier than if Schmidt said it.

jokes.text: It's arguably, like, an airplane throwing up.
jokes.setup: Schmidt's mom is furious about the penis graffiti drawn into his childhood photo
jokes.punchline: Schmidt offers an alternative visual interpretation — 'arguably, like, an airplane throwing up' — with complete seriousness, trying to reframe an ejaculating penis as aviation nausea
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the reel. The word 'arguably' does enormous work — Schmidt genuinely believes this interpretation has merit and is willing to defend it. 'An airplane throwing up' is a brilliantly specific, innocent re-reading that only someone desperately trying to un-see a penis would generate. High originality because this exact joke could not have been written by formula — it required someone finding the most absurd but geometrically defensible alternative. Highly quotable, works completely out of context.

jokes.text: You think I don't know that's a dick and balls? I know all about dick and balls! I partied with Robert Downey Jr. before he got sober, when he was really fucked up and a lot of fun!
jokes.setup: Schmidt tries to convince his mom the graffiti is an airplane; she rejects the interpretation
jokes.punchline: She asserts her knowledge of phallic imagery, then immediately pivots to establishing her wild-past credibility via a very specific Robert Downey Jr. anecdote — connecting genitalia expertise to celebrity partying as proof of worldliness
jokes.explanation: The non-sequitur pivot from 'I know dick and balls' to 'I partied with Robert Downey Jr. before he got sober' is a genuinely surprising and original joke. The specificity of 'before he got sober, when he was really fucked up and a lot of fun' is both a perfect character revelation (the mom has a past) and a darkly funny commentary on RDJ's well-known history. This is the kind of celebrity reference that earns its laugh through the twist rather than name-dropping alone.

jokes.text: From now on, you're gonna do some chores. You're gonna wash the laundry, you're gonna fold it, you're gonna do the dishes, you're gonna mow the lawn...
jokes.setup: An adult is punishing Schmidt, who is an undercover cop in his late 20s
jokes.punchline: The punishment is a list of household chores — an adult cop is being grounded like a teenager, which he has to accept
jokes.explanation: Good sustained irony — a cop being punished with chores. The comedy is in Schmidt having to accept it. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Dude, I have a surprise for you. Last night at the party, I took Eric's phone and I had Zack put this monitoring device in it...
jokes.setup: Schmidt is being scolded at home; Jenko arrives with exciting news
jokes.punchline: Jenko has actually done something competent and clever for once — the joke is Schmidt's begrudging reaction ('I'm glad you have something to do') and his inability to simply be happy for Jenko
jokes.explanation: More of a plot beat than a joke, but Schmidt's passive-aggressive 'I'm glad you have something to do' is a solid character moment. The competence/incompetence dynamic between the two is the engine of a lot of the film's comedy.

jokes.text: Password! / Kneel before Zod! / You may enter. / Thank you, Zod.
jokes.setup: Jenko arrives at Zack's secret lab/room with a password system
jokes.punchline: 'Kneel before Zod' (from Superman II) as a lab password is absurd enough, but 'Thank you, Zod' — Jenko thanking the fictional villain for letting him in — adds an extra layer of sincere reverence for the bit
jokes.explanation: The 'Thank you, Zod' is the hidden gem — it's not in the script of Superman II, it's Jenko completely inhabiting the fiction of the password exchange. Character-specific nerd humor that works on multiple levels.

jokes.text: Let's tap that wire, huh? / We were just about to go outside with a bunch of chemicals. We were going to test what blows up. / There's no reason the wiretap is super urgent, right?
jokes.setup: Jenko wants to monitor the wiretap they set up on Eric's phone
jokes.punchline: Zack casually mentions they were about to go outside and test what chemicals blow up — framing the most dangerous activity imaginable as a reasonable alternative to the urgent police work
jokes.explanation: Good character-specific comedy — Zack is clearly a science nerd whose idea of fun is literally explosive experiments. The deadpan delivery of 'test what blows up' as a competing priority to police wiretapping is funny in its casualness.

jokes.text: Yes! / Yes, that's what I'm talking about! / That's what I'm talking about! / I love this science shit! / This is what you guys do all day? Let's do it again.
jokes.setup: Zack's chemical experiment blows something up
jokes.punchline: Jenko's pure childlike joy at a controlled explosion — 'I love this science shit! This is what you guys do all day?' — reveals that the former bully/jock has found his tribe among the science kids
jokes.explanation: Excellent character work. Jenko finding genuine joy in nerd science is the film's secondary emotional arc (the reversal of high school roles), and this moment nails it comedically. 'I love this science shit!' is a great Jenko line — enthusiastic, slightly dim, completely sincere.

jokes.text: Are you texting Molly? / What? I don't... Molly... / Maybe. Is that... / Whoa, it's cool, man, come on. / I'm not some, like, '50s letterman who pins a girl. / I mean, yeah, we blow each other sometimes, but it's not a thing. / I just, like... I don't know, I don't believe in possessions, ja feel?
jokes.setup: Jenko catches Schmidt texting Molly; Schmidt is caught out and embarrassed
jokes.punchline: Eric materializes and casually reveals he has a physical relationship with Molly but 'doesn't believe in possessions' — delivered with hippie-bro philosophy while completely torpedoing Schmidt's romantic hopes
jokes.explanation: Eric's philosophy of non-possessiveness applied to sexual relationships with casual 'ja feel?' is excellent character work and cringe comedy — it's deeply uncomfortable for Schmidt while Eric is completely at ease. 'I don't believe in possessions' as justification for a friends-with-benefits setup is a perfect piece of eco-hippie-bro characterization. Rewatch bonus for how well Eric's oblivious delivery lands against Schmidt's visible devastation.

jokes.text: Ja feel, ja definitely feel.
jokes.setup: Eric uses the hip slang 'ja feel?' — Schmidt has just been told his crush 'blows' the drug dealer
jokes.punchline: Schmidt's desperate, overeager 'ja definitely feel' is a reaction beat — he's dying inside but performing cool
jokes.explanation: The gap between what Schmidt must feel emotionally and his desperate performance of agreement is excellent cringe-comedy. 'Ja definitely feel' — the addition of 'definitely' revealing his overcompensation — is a subtle but effective detail. Good economy.

jokes.text: Ja feel, ja definitely feel.
jokes.setup: Eric delivers his philosophy of non-possession regarding Molly and asks 'ja feel?'
jokes.punchline: Schmidt, clearly devastated, responds with an over-emphatic 'ja definitely feel' — the doubling of the affirmation while he clearly does NOT feel okay is a perfect straight-man reaction
jokes.explanation: Three words that contain multitudes. Schmidt's 'ja definitely feel' is both an adoption of Eric's vocabulary (necessary for undercover work) and a barely-concealed emotional meltdown. Economy score very high because this response communicates pain, professionalism, and character all at once.

jokes.text: Hey. How are you? / How is my favorite police officer? / Your mother told me that you are undercover. / Are you undercover right now? / Yes, it means I'm undercover right now. / Are those the bad guys over there? Do they have guns? Oh, my God. Oh, God, this is so exciting. I have got to call Annie. She is gonna die.
jokes.setup: An older neighbor woman (Phyllis) recognizes Schmidt while he's undercover near Eric and the science kids
jokes.punchline: She immediately announces his undercover status, escalates to identifying 'the bad guys,' and decides to call her friend Annie about the excitement — completely destroying his cover in real time
jokes.explanation: Classic comedy of well-meaning catastrophe. Each of Phyllis's reactions escalates the danger while she remains completely oblivious: identifying the target ('are those the bad guys?'), announcing the assignment ('you are undercover'), and planning to spread the news ('I have got to call Annie'). Well-structured escalation with a good specific detail in 'She is gonna die.'

jokes.text: Shut your fucking mouth. / Shut your fucking mouth, you understand me? / Let's go check this out. / I will straight-up punch you in the face if you do not shut up. / There is no... / A straight-up face punch. / I swear to God, you're gonna get me killed.
jokes.setup: Schmidt tries desperately to silence Phyllis before she blows his cover
jokes.punchline: Schmidt issues increasingly aggressive threats to an elderly woman — 'straight-up punch you in the face' — while she cheerfully ignores him and continues to be excited about 'checking this out'
jokes.explanation: Schmidt threatening to punch an old lady for being too enthusiastic is a great inversion of the cover-blown scene. 'A straight-up face punch' as a repeated emphasis is funny because it sounds more absurd with each repetition. The gap between Schmidt's desperation and Phyllis's cheerful obliviousness is the engine.

jokes.text: Shit! She just tried to grab my dick, dude! / What? You tried to grab his... / She tried to grab my junk. She was like, 'Oh, my God, I have arthritis, it hurts my hand, I need to grab a handful of that dick.' / I was like, 'Get the fuck off me!'
jokes.setup: Schmidt escapes the Phyllis situation and finds Jenko
jokes.punchline: He reports that Phyllis groped him, then provides a full 'quote' of her alleged justification — 'I have arthritis, it hurts my hand, I need to grab a handful of that dick' — a completely invented-sounding excuse that escalates the absurdity
jokes.explanation: The quoted justification is the comedic peak — 'I have arthritis, it hurts my hand, I need to grab a handful of that dick' is so specific and logically broken that it becomes very funny. The arthritis-to-groping medical reasoning is absurdist at its best. High quotability because the quote is so specific and odd.

jokes.text: She said, 'I need to grab a handful of that dick'? / And it felt good, but then it felt weird for a second, so I pushed her.
jokes.setup: Jenko processes the Phyllis groping story
jokes.punchline: Schmidt admits it 'felt good' briefly before he realized the context — the honest confession of momentary enjoyment of an elderly woman's grope, followed by immediate disgust and physical rejection
jokes.explanation: The admission 'it felt good, but then it felt weird' is a devastating comedic beat — Schmidt's honest moment of physiological response before cognition caught up is both very human and extremely funny. The structure is excellent: confession, qualification, consequence ('so I pushed her'). Jonah Hill's delivery of this kind of mortified honesty is a signature skill, and this is one of the best uses of it in the reel.

jokes.text: You're so lucky your parents don't give a shit about you. / Right?
jokes.setup: Molly mentions her parents are out most nights and are 'laissez-faire'; Schmidt responds
jokes.punchline: Schmidt frames parental neglect as enviable luck — a sincere compliment about absent parents, delivered as genuine admiration, that reveals his smothering home life as its own tragedy
jokes.explanation: Sharp dark comedy in a compact line. 'You're so lucky your parents don't give a shit about you' as sincere admiration is a great ironic inversion — Schmidt so suffocated by love that neglect seems idyllic. Molly's 'Right?' in agreement adds to the casual darkness. Very economical.

jokes.text: You're so lucky your parents don't give a shit about you. / Right?
jokes.setup: Someone is admiring Molly's freedom to have parties while parents are out
jokes.punchline: Calling neglectful parenting 'lucky' — the teenager's perspective that absent parents are aspirational — is an ironic but authentic teen-logic observation
jokes.explanation: Sharp ironic observation that feels authentic to teenage logic. 'You're so lucky your parents don't give a shit about you' is a quotable line that lands because it's both true to adolescent thinking and subtly dark. Good economy.

jokes.text: Sorry. I'm happy to see you. / Yeah. Yeah, me, too. [awkward beat as they process a bigger-than-expected hug]
jokes.setup: Schmidt arrives and Molly gives him an unexpectedly enthusiastic hug
jokes.punchline: Both acknowledge the hug was more than expected; the shared awkward recognition and over-earnest 'Yeah, me too' imply romantic feelings that neither is ready to address
jokes.explanation: Sweet awkward moment. The comedy is in the physical surprise and mutual recognition — more charming than hilarious. Works as a tonal beat.

jokes.text: I brought tacos, so that's cool. / Try to turn it, try to turn it, spoiler alert / Spoiler alert, spoiler alert!
jokes.setup: Schmidt tries to pivot from an awkward romantic moment with Molly
jokes.punchline: 'I brought tacos, so that's cool' is a spectacularly anti-climactic way to follow a charged emotional beat; then 'spoiler alert' used urgently about something trivial continues the bathos
jokes.explanation: 'I brought tacos, so that's cool' is a lovely awkward deflection — the specificity of tacos as a romantic-moment-ender is good. The 'spoiler alert' escalation is weaker but adds energy.

jokes.text: Hey, boys, this eco-pussy is going down today. / Take down eco-pussy / Take down eco-pussy!
jokes.setup: Jenko is pumped up for the wiretap operation targeting Eric
jokes.punchline: Jenko's battle cry reduces their target to 'eco-pussy' — a compound insult that merges Eric's environmentalist persona with an emasculating slur, delivered with complete enthusiasm
jokes.explanation: 'Eco-pussy' as a character descriptor is a good portmanteau insult that efficiently encapsulates Eric as a target. Jenko's enthusiasm for his own coinage is very in-character. Somewhat crude but specific to the film's vocabulary.

jokes.text: Try to turn it, try to turn it, spoiler alert / Spoiler alert, spoiler alert!
jokes.setup: Someone is trying to manage a moment before it goes wrong
jokes.punchline: 'Spoiler alert' deployed as a warning that something bad/embarrassing is about to happen — meta-awareness of narrative beats
jokes.explanation: Mild meta-language joke. 'Spoiler alert' used to signal upcoming embarrassment is functional internet-era comedy but not especially crafted. Context is slightly unclear from transcript.

jokes.text: Mother Earth, Mother Earth is dying / And when it rains / It means that beautiful bitch is crying
jokes.setup: Eric is overheard performing/singing an eco-protest song
jokes.punchline: The song's environmental message is sincere but the metaphor ('beautiful bitch is crying') is so clunky and the earnest delivery so at odds with the content that it becomes comedy
jokes.explanation: Eric's musical eco-activism is perfect character comedy — the song is bad eco-protest music delivered by someone who thinks it's profound. 'Beautiful bitch is crying' as a lyric is excellent because it tries to be both reverent and edgy and fails at both. High character integration: only Eric would write this song.

jokes.text: Hey, boys, this eco-pussy is going down today. / Take down eco-pussy / Take down eco-pussy!
jokes.setup: Jenko has been successfully inducted into Eric's eco-activist circle as an undercover operative
jokes.punchline: He privately celebrates their plan to 'take down eco-pussy' — using Eric's own eco-warrior framing against him in a crude nickname
jokes.explanation: 'Eco-pussy' as a nickname for Eric is consistent with Jenko's crudeness and plays nicely against Eric's earnest environmentalism. The rallying-cry repetition with Schmidt is a good energy beat. Decent character comedy.

jokes.text: It's really not a planet. / It's for sure a planet. / Pluto is a planet. / It used to be a planet. / It's ready! / Not any more.
jokes.setup: In the background, while Eric performs his eco-song, there's a debate about Pluto's planetary status
jokes.punchline: The Pluto debate — 'it's ready!' announced in the middle of their astronomical disagreement — creates a comedic juxtaposition: the trivial cosmic argument persists even as a police operation reaches its crucial moment
jokes.explanation: Good layered comedy: the Pluto debate is both a character beat (Zack is definitely a Pluto-is-a-planet person) and a structural comic contrast with the wiretap operation reaching readiness. The timing of 'It's ready!' cutting into the debate is a nice comic edit.

jokes.text: Reduce, reuse / Recycle / I'm embarrassed. / I always feel exposed after playing. / Do not feel exposed.
jokes.setup: Eric finishes his eco-protest song to a small audience
jokes.punchline: Eric's post-performance vulnerability ('I always feel exposed after playing') is treated with complete sincerity by Molly, while the song itself was objectively embarrassing — the gap between Eric's artistic self-perception and reality is the joke
jokes.explanation: Eric's earnest post-performance vulnerability about a genuinely bad song is a solid cringe beat. 'I always feel exposed after playing' is delivered as though he's a serious artist, which is funnier than if he were joking about it.

jokes.text: I'm embarrassed. / I always feel exposed after playing.
jokes.setup: Eric has just finished his earnest eco-performance
jokes.punchline: His post-performance vulnerability — 'I always feel exposed after playing' — parodies sincere artistic self-disclosure, but said by someone whose art is objectively embarrassing
jokes.explanation: 'I always feel exposed after playing' is a parody of sincere-artist vulnerability — the kind of thing said by genuine performers, delivered here with complete earnestness about an eco-activist song. Good character integration.

jokes.text: All right, all right, all right, all right. God damn that. / The mic is live and we can hear how the other half lives.
jokes.setup: The wiretap finally goes live just as Eric's humiliating song ends
jokes.punchline: Jenko's triumphant 'God damn that' and his framing of eavesdropping on a drug dealer as hearing 'how the other half lives' — as though Eric's lifestyle is exotic and aspirational rather than embarrassing
jokes.explanation: 'How the other half lives' applied to a teen eco-drug-dealer doing bad folk music is a good ironic kicker to close the reel. Jenko's genuine enthusiasm for the operation is in character and provides a solid energetic ending beat.

jokes.text: Yeah, no, I feel the same way about you, except girl version. You're a girl.
jokes.setup: Molly sincerely says Schmidt is a good guy and she cares about him
jokes.punchline: Schmidt returns the sentiment but lands on the deeply obvious observation that she is, in fact, a girl
jokes.explanation: Classic Schmidt awkwardness — his social incompetence causes him to laboriously explain the obvious. The self-correction 'except girl version. You're a girl.' is a nicely structured comedic stumble that feels true to the character.

jokes.text: That's why I put this dress on, to remind you.
jokes.setup: Schmidt has just awkwardly stated the obvious that she is a girl
jokes.punchline: Molly dryly plays along, pretending the dress is a memo to Schmidt about her gender
jokes.explanation: Very economical comeback — she doesn't oversell it, just deadpans a wry confirmation. The brevity and dryness make it land cleanly.

jokes.text: No hesitash.
jokes.setup: Schmidt is enthusiastically affirming Molly's excitement about the play
jokes.punchline: He truncates 'hesitation' to 'hesitash' — a nonsense abbreviation that reveals his verbal awkwardness under pressure
jokes.explanation: A small but effective verbal tic joke — Schmidt's social anxiety manifests in a word he can't quite finish. Character-specific and efficiently delivered.

jokes.text: What a vagina. He has no chance with her.
jokes.setup: Jenko watches Schmidt fumble through a sweet moment with Molly
jokes.punchline: Jenko's blunt, crude commentary undercuts the romantic scene entirely
jokes.explanation: Functional Jenko commentary — crude but on-brand. The irony of him being completely wrong about Schmidt's chances gives it mild retroactive value but it's not especially inventive in isolation.

jokes.text: Prom eats a dong. Multiple dongs.
jokes.setup: Molly says she thinks prom is going to be awesome; Jenko riffs on his disdain for prom
jokes.punchline: He upgrades from 'eats a dong' to 'multiple dongs' — a pointless but committed escalation
jokes.explanation: The self-escalation to 'multiple dongs' is a sharp little joke — it implies Jenko thought 'one dong' was insufficient emphasis and needed to quantify his contempt. Very Jenko.

jokes.text: Who we gonna take to the prom? No one's going to prom with us... You pull up in a white stallion of a limo. Doves fly out behind you, slow motion.
jokes.setup: Jenko just said prom eats a dong, then immediately pivots to fantasizing about the perfect prom night
jokes.punchline: His elaborate prom fantasy — complete with doves in slow motion — contradicts his dismissal perfectly; he cares deeply about prom
jokes.explanation: This is excellent character comedy — Jenko's instant U-turn from contempt to earnest romanticism is completely in character with his emotional immaturity. 'Doves fly out behind you, slow motion' is a genuinely funny image that escalates the absurdity. The whole beat earns its length.

jokes.text: Doves. Why doves? 'Cause doves make you look like a badass, that's why.
jokes.setup: Jenko includes doves in his prom fantasy
jokes.punchline: Schmidt questions the doves; Jenko has a completely confident and completely insane justification ready
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best small exchanges. The two-line structure is perfect: question, then absurd-but-confident answer delivered with zero irony. Jenko's certainty that doves = badass is a pure distillation of his character. Highly quotable and compact — maximum funny per word. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: Aren't... Isn't... Aren't you and Eric... Wouldn't you and Eric go together? Not that I know of.
jokes.setup: Schmidt wants to ask Molly to prom but is terrified; he tries to establish whether she's going with Eric
jokes.punchline: His spectacular verbal stumbling through three false starts followed by Molly's matter-of-fact 'Not that I know of' — which opens the door he can't walk through
jokes.explanation: The comedy of Schmidt's verbal collapse is effective cringe, well-performed. Molly's cool response is the perfect straight-man beat. The humor is in the gap between his anxiety and the simplicity of what he's trying to say.

jokes.text: He's going to choke. He always chokes. He's going to choke, wait for it.
jokes.setup: Schmidt is visibly struggling to ask Molly to prom while Jenko watches from afar
jokes.punchline: Jenko's running color commentary, delivered like a sports announcer calling a choke, is both accurate and brutally unsympathetic
jokes.explanation: The repetition of 'he's going to choke' has a good rhythm and Jenko's detached glee in his friend's suffering is very true to the character dynamic. 'Wait for it' gives it a nice comic beat.

jokes.text: That is the actual sound of choking.
jokes.setup: Schmidt actually makes an audible choking/gagging sound mid-sentence while trying to ask Molly out
jokes.punchline: Jenko's dry literal observation that this is, technically, the actual sound of choking
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — six words that land hard because they literalize the metaphor ('choking') just used. The callback to his own prediction is tight. It's a great button on the choking sequence.

jokes.text: Would you want to go to me... Maybe with me to prom? / Yes. / What? She just said yes! / Good for you, Doug.
jokes.setup: After multiple failed attempts, Schmidt finally scrambles out a barely coherent prom invitation
jokes.punchline: Molly says yes immediately; Jenko's incredulous 'What? She just said yes!' and sincere 'Good for you, Doug' — the latter being both funny and oddly sweet
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the extended prom-asking sequence works because it subverts Jenko's confident prediction. His shocked disbelief followed by genuine pride in Schmidt is the right emotional beat. 'Good for you, Doug' lands because it's both funny and actually warm.

jokes.text: He's adopted. We all suspect from a very lame family.
jokes.setup: Someone asks Eric about Schmidt ('Doug'), noting they look totally different for 'brothers'
jokes.punchline: Eric says he's adopted, then adds the kicker: 'from a very lame family' — a casual brutal dismissal
jokes.explanation: The two-part structure works: the cover story answer, then the unprompted insult tag. Not especially original but efficiently delivered. Eric's casual cruelty is consistent with his characterization.

jokes.text: You know how Tom Cruise is always pissed off at Rain Man? That's like my life, except Brad is really shitty at math.
jokes.setup: Eric is explaining his relationship with Schmidt to someone, using a pop-culture reference
jokes.punchline: He inverts the Rain Man dynamic — his 'Rain Man' isn't even good at math, the one thing that would make it worth it
jokes.explanation: This is a genuinely well-constructed joke. The Rain Man reference isn't just a name-drop — it's deployed with a specific twist that adds comedic logic: Rain Man is tolerable because of the math superpower. Remove that, and you're left with pure burden. The economy is excellent. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Your brother's kind of a dick. / Well, yeah. He kind of is, isn't he? / Don't listen to that. I don't give a fuck.
jokes.setup: Schmidt has just heard Eric trash-talk him to his face (while Eric thinks Schmidt is 'Brad,' the loser brother)
jokes.punchline: Schmidt agreeing that his own cover-identity's 'brother' is a dick, then immediately telling himself not to care — but clearly caring
jokes.explanation: The situational irony — Schmidt is both insulted and cannot react — works. The self-pep-talk 'I don't give a fuck' that obviously means he does give a fuck is a believable character moment.

jokes.text: You failed to stop the outbreak, and you have no leads! We are running out of time! You either find the supplier, or I'm gonna jump your asses off Jump Street!
jokes.setup: Captain Dickson berates Schmidt and Jenko for their failure on the case
jokes.punchline: 'I'm gonna jump your asses off Jump Street' — a meta threat that uses the show's own title as a verb/threat
jokes.explanation: Ice Cube weaponizing the film's title as a threat is a fun bit of meta self-awareness. His delivery makes it land. The escalating fury of the speech sets the punchline up well.

jokes.text: Is that a code for sex?
jokes.setup: Schmidt explains his lead involves a 'stuffed piñata' — a phrase that sounds absurd out of context
jokes.punchline: Dickson's deadpan 'Is that a code for sex?' — delivered by Ice Cube with magnificent blankness
jokes.explanation: Five words, perfectly placed. The joke works on two levels: (1) the piñata detail IS absurd enough to sound like slang, (2) Dickson's mind going to 'sex' first is a great character reveal. Ice Cube's deadpan delivery elevates it. Near-perfect economy. One of the reel's best one-liners.

jokes.text: Remember that wiretap I put on Eric's phone? While you were having the time of your life last night, I was listening.
jokes.setup: Jenko explains how he got the piñata lead
jokes.punchline: The implied contrast — Schmidt was presumably doing something fun while Jenko was alone listening to a wiretap — delivered with injured pride
jokes.explanation: Jenko's wounded martyr act is mildly amusing and consistent with the film's buddy dynamic. Functional but not among the reel's stronger moments.

jokes.text: I apologize in advance if I throw up on you onstage.
jokes.setup: Molly is nervous before the school play premiere
jokes.punchline: She offers the advance apology for a grotesque but specific possibility — vomiting on a castmate — with complete matter-of-factness
jokes.explanation: Specific and pleasantly gross. The advance apology framing is a nice structure — she's not saying she might throw up, she's pre-apologizing, which implies it's a known risk. Efficient and charming.

jokes.text: Is it too sexy of an outfit? Bend the knee a little bit. Yep, it is.
jokes.setup: Schmidt is in his Peter Pan costume; Molly asks if it's too sexy
jokes.punchline: Schmidt does a quick knee-bend test and definitively confirms: yes, it is too sexy — implying the costume is hilariously revealing on him
jokes.explanation: The physical test protocol is funny — Schmidt devises an instant knee-bend diagnostic for sexiness, confirms the worst, and reports it clinically. Visual gag that works even on the page.

jokes.text: Potassium nitrate / Don't hate. It's great... If you can't respect that, you're a butt muncher... K-NO-three, don't give no grief. / It can be used to make corned beef.
jokes.setup: Schmidt performs his science rap for the school play, in full Peter Pan costume
jokes.punchline: The rap is aggressively dorky, rhymes 'potassium nitrate' with 'don't hate. It's great,' hits a baffling 'butt muncher' insult for non-believers, and concludes corned beef is a key use of an explosive oxidizer
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's comedic highlights. The science rap is perfectly calibrated: each line is worse than the last, the threats ('butt muncher') are gloriously unhinged, and 'K-NO-three, don't give no grief / It can be used to make corned beef' is genuinely inspired absurdist writing. Deeply character-specific — only Schmidt would go this hard on a school science rap while wearing Peter Pan tights. High quotability, strong rewatch value.

jokes.text: Potassium nitrate. Thanks for noticing.
jokes.setup: Jenko sees Schmidt in his Peter Pan/chemistry rap costume and says 'Whoa, what are you wearing?'
jokes.punchline: Schmidt identifies the costume by its science content and thanks Jenko for the acknowledgment — completely missing the implied criticism
jokes.explanation: Four words, maximum efficiency. Schmidt's oblivious pride — identifying himself by the chemical he's dressed as, then thanking someone for 'noticing' — is a perfect character beat. The deadpan delivery of absurd logic is exactly what the film does best.

jokes.text: Is that code for a sex thing?
jokes.setup: Jenko tells Schmidt his piñata is 'killing him' — the drug deal piñata is apparently moving
jokes.punchline: Schmidt echoes Dickson's earlier 'Is that a code for sex?' question almost verbatim — now a running gag
jokes.explanation: Smart callback — Schmidt unknowingly mirrors Dickson's exact confusion. The gag is that 'stuffed piñata' genuinely does sound like slang. The running gag structure elevates both instances.

jokes.text: What did I say? What did I say? See? Whose wiretap is working for him now, huh?
jokes.setup: Jenko had placed a wiretap and is now proven right that it was useful; he milks the vindication
jokes.punchline: His triumph is completely disproportionate to the moment — 'whose wiretap is working for him now' is a weirdly specific piece of gloating
jokes.explanation: Jenko's compulsive need to be validated is a consistent character note. The specificity of 'whose wiretap' — referring to the tool, not himself — is a funny quirk of the phrasing.

jokes.text: You told me not to worry about the tickets! I thought they made us look cool. / Cones, cones... Driver's ed car. / I'm driving. / No, you're not. / I never get to drive. I'm driving this time. / Fine! Drive!
jokes.setup: In their rush to follow the drug deal, Schmidt and Jenko commandeer a driver's ed car
jokes.punchline: Their urgent car chase is immediately derailed by an absurd argument about who gets to drive the teacher-brake-equipped car
jokes.explanation: Classic action-comedy deflation — an urgent situation interrupted by a petty domestic argument. 'I never get to drive' is a perfect childish grievance deployed in a car chase. The driver's ed car as the chase vehicle is an inspired absurd premise.

jokes.text: If they see us, just pretend like you're sucking my dick. / What? No! / Why am I automatically blowing you? / 'Cause you're in a fucking Peter Pan costume!
jokes.setup: They need to hide from drug dealers in the parking lot; Jenko proposes a cover
jokes.punchline: Schmidt's grievance isn't the act itself but the assumption that he's the one doing it — Jenko's answer ('because you're in a Peter Pan costume') is a perfect absurdist non-sequitur that somehow works as logic
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the reel. The structure is immaculate: the outrageous suggestion, Schmidt's protest about role assignment (not the act), and the callback to the Peter Pan costume as sufficient logical justification. 'Why am I automatically blowing you?' is a perfect line — the word 'automatically' does so much work, implying this is a recurring hierarchical assumption. Jenko's costume-based reasoning is absurdist but internally consistent. Very quotable, strong rewatch value. Approaches the 8.0 anchor benchmark.

jokes.text: Dude, did you just hit the teacher brake? / Yeah, you're following too close, dude.
jokes.setup: They're in the driver's ed car following drug dealers; Jenko is driving too close
jokes.punchline: Schmidt hits the passenger-side teacher brake, then justifies it perfectly — the car's inherent safety feature becomes a comedic beat
jokes.explanation: Smart use of the driver's ed car premise — the teacher brake is both a funny visual and a character expression (Schmidt's anxious control-freakery). The gag gets more from the car's inherent comedy than a generic vehicle would.

jokes.text: Seriously, if you do that again, I'm going to Whac-A-Mole you in the balls.
jokes.setup: Schmidt keeps hitting the teacher brake; Jenko threatens him
jokes.punchline: The threat is 'Whac-A-Mole you in the balls' — an oddly specific and evocative image that merges the childhood game with genital violence
jokes.explanation: Genuinely original threat phrasing. 'Whac-A-Mole you in the balls' is an unexpected combination — the specificity of the game reference creates a vivid and funny image. Very quotable. This is Jenko's voice at its best: childlike reference, adult violence.

jokes.text: What the fuck? You non-driving motherfuckers! Get the fuck out of the car! / What are you, a fucking Keebler Elf? / It's fucking ZZ Top! / Like an angry walrus! / I stomp the car now!
jokes.setup: Schmidt and Jenko cause an accident; the driver of the other car goes completely berserk
jokes.punchline: The road rage sequence escalates through increasingly absurd insults ('Keebler Elf,' 'ZZ Top,' 'angry walrus') and culminates in the man literally stomping their car
jokes.explanation: The escalating insult sequence is very funny — each comparison is more surreal than the last, and 'I stomp the car now!' (grammatically broken, as if he's narrating a Godzilla movie) is a great button. The visual of a man actually stomping a car adds physical comedy. High impact as a set piece.

jokes.text: I can't! I'm wearing tights! / I got skinny jeans on! It's the same fucking thing!
jokes.setup: They need to run from danger but Schmidt is in his Peter Pan tights
jokes.punchline: Jenko's immediate equivalence between Peter Pan tights and skinny jeans — and his rage that this is 'the same fucking thing' — is both a fashion observation and character comedy
jokes.explanation: Sharp two-line exchange. Schmidt's tights-based mobility complaint is immediately turned back on Jenko via skinny jeans — a perfect character reveal (Jenko wears skinny jeans) and a funny fashion-equality argument ('it's the same fucking thing') delivered with genuine fury. Very quotable. One of the reel's best quick exchanges.

jokes.text: Police! Get out of the car, douche! / I'm on a call here, jackass. / That's right. Go to sleep, bitch. You just got head-butted, motherfucker!
jokes.setup: Jenko carjacks a Porsche during the chase; the driver resists
jokes.punchline: The driver is calmly on a phone call; Jenko head-butts him, then delivers a triumphant villain monologue to an unconscious man
jokes.explanation: The 'I'm on a call here, jackass' from the victim is a perfect mundane-vs-chaos beat. Jenko's triumphant narration of his own head-butt to an unconscious person is classic overcelebration. The specificity of 'you just got head-butted' (stating exactly what happened) adds to it.

jokes.text: Where? Where? There's no glove compartment in this shitty-ass car! There's golf balls and this. / What am I supposed to do with this? / I don't know, man! I've never been in a freeway chase before!
jokes.setup: In the stolen Porsche, Jenko asks Schmidt to find a gun in the glove compartment
jokes.punchline: There's no glove compartment; Schmidt finds only golf balls and an unspecified object; Jenko's admission that he has no experience with freeway chases
jokes.explanation: 'I've never been in a freeway chase before' is a great confession of incompetence in the middle of a freeway chase. The golf balls are a nice absurdist detail. The sequence works as an escalating panic routine.

jokes.text: Watch out! It's going to explode! It's going to go! / What happened? / I don't know. / It just didn't explode. / That's weird.
jokes.setup: They throw something at the pursuers, convinced it will explode
jokes.punchline: It doesn't explode; they both calmly observe 'That's weird' and move on — complete deflation of action-movie expectation
jokes.explanation: A deliberate subversion of action movie conventions — the thing doesn't explode, and no one has an explanation. 'That's weird' is the perfect deadpan response to a non-explosion. The film is openly deconstructing genre clichés here. This gets funnier on rewatch because you know it's coming. The later callback (joke 33) when it finally DOES explode amplifies it retroactively.

jokes.text: Can anybody tell me where my Peter is?
jokes.setup: Chaos is happening; the drama teacher runs onto the scene looking for the actor playing Peter Pan
jokes.punchline: 'Where is my Peter?' is an accidental double entendre that the teacher is completely unaware of
jokes.explanation: Classic accidental double entendre. The setup is there — Peter Pan is missing — but the joke type is fairly obvious. It's efficiently deployed and gets a laugh, but it's not the most original beat in the reel.

jokes.text: Oh, gosh. And I've been in character for months now. / Great. Nobody cares.
jokes.setup: French Samuels is told he has to go on as Peter Pan despite not being prepared
jokes.punchline: French mentions he's been 'in character for months' — a comically committed acting-student detail; teacher's 'Nobody cares' is a brutal and funny dismissal
jokes.explanation: The 'in character for months' detail is the kind of hyper-specific commitment that's very funny — it implies a truly intense drama-kid devotion. The teacher's callous dismissal is the right contrast. Economical and character-revealing.

jokes.text: I'm sorry I didn't check the traffic report before we got in a car chase!
jokes.setup: They're stuck in traffic during a car chase and Schmidt is frustrated
jokes.punchline: Jenko's sarcastic apology for not accounting for traffic during an improvised freeway chase is a perfectly absurd complaint
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the absurd logic: Schmidt is treating a car chase like a commute where you should have checked Waze. Jenko's sarcastic apology for the oversight is very funny because it frames the chase as a failure of planning rather than a lawless emergency. Good economy.

jokes.text: Are you texting? / No, I'm not texting! / Yes, you are! You're texting! / No, I'm not! / Okay, almost done. [text message sound: IILOL.ll]
jokes.setup: They are in a freeway car chase; Jenko accuses Schmidt of texting
jokes.punchline: Schmidt denies it repeatedly, then admits 'almost done' — he is absolutely texting during a car chase
jokes.explanation: Perfectly structured lie-exposure: denial, escalating denial, then immediate capitulation ('okay, almost done'). The juxtaposition of texting etiquette in a gunfight is funny. The structure — building the denial then completely collapsing it — is clean and effective.

jokes.text: Why do you always jump over the car like that? / Hi. Hi. How are you? / God damn, you are beautiful. You are fine as shit. / Don't worry. Someone will pick you up. / Wait. Pick me up?
jokes.setup: In the middle of a freeway chase, Jenko jumps over a stopped car and pauses to hit on a woman inside
jokes.punchline: He tells her 'someone will pick you up' — she thinks he's flirting, but he's literally referring to the traffic — then immediately sprints away, leaving her confused
jokes.explanation: Classic Jenko — his libido survives a gunfight. The double meaning of 'someone will pick you up' (flirt vs. literal traffic comment) is an accidental double entendre that the film lets breathe. Schmidt's 'why do you always jump over the car like that?' implies this is a Jenko habit, which is an even funnier detail.

jokes.text: Why don't you text them and ask them to stop chasing us?
jokes.setup: They're being chased; Jenko needs a plan
jokes.punchline: He suggests texting their pursuers — a callback to Schmidt texting during the chase — with mock-sincere sarcasm
jokes.explanation: Quick and efficient callback. The suggestion is absurd but follows a weird logic given Schmidt was just texting. Economy is excellent — one sentence does the callback and the new joke simultaneously.

jokes.text: I'm going to throw this thing at him! / Okay, you don't have to narrate everything! / Just throw it!
jokes.setup: Jenko is about to throw something at a pursuer
jokes.punchline: Schmidt's complaint isn't the danger — it's that Jenko is narrating his own actions in real time
jokes.explanation: 'You don't have to narrate everything' is a great mid-action complaint — the specificity of the criticism (not 'stop, it's dangerous' but 'stop giving a play-by-play') is very funny and character-revealing. Jenko's self-narration is a believable action-hero affectation.

jokes.text: I really thought that one was going to explode.
jokes.setup: Second explosion attempt also fails; both characters regroup
jokes.punchline: Jenko's sincere, almost wistful statement that he was really sure this one would explode
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best understated beats. The deadpan sincerity of Jenko's disappointment — delivered as genuine emotional investment in the explosion — is perfect. The film has now committed to the non-exploding-things gag as a running bit, and this line is its best expression. 'I really thought that one' implies he has updated his priors and was still wrong. Maximum economy.

jokes.text: What are you talking about? We're in a pink Bug! / I don't care. Look in the goddamn glove compartment! / What the hell?
jokes.setup: Jenko tells Schmidt to look in the glove compartment for a gun — they have now commandeered a Volkswagen Beetle
jokes.punchline: Schmidt points out they're in a pink Bug — the least intimidating vehicle imaginable for a drug chase; there is nonetheless something in the glove compartment
jokes.explanation: The pink Bug is a great visual comedy detail — it's the specific absurdity of the vehicle that makes it funny. The fact that there IS something in the glove compartment of the Bug is a good setup for the next beat.

jokes.text: What the hell? [gun found in pink Bug glove compartment]
jokes.setup: Schmidt predicted the pink Bug would not have a gun; Jenko insisted he look
jokes.punchline: There is in fact a gun in the pink Bug's glove compartment — Schmidt's 'What the hell?' is genuine bafflement that the absurd logic worked
