jokes.explanation: Perfect subversion: the clearly correct prediction (no gun) is wrong, which validates Jenko's idiot logic and undermines Schmidt's reasonable skepticism. 'What the hell?' as a reaction to being wrong in the best possible way is a funny beat. Good misdirection.

jokes.text: That's what exploded? Holy shit. That was crazy.
jokes.setup: After multiple non-explosions, something finally does explode
jokes.punchline: Their shocked reaction to the eventual explosion — after having been let down twice — is a perfect payoff to the running non-explosion gag
jokes.explanation: Perfect payoff to the running non-explosion bit. The structure — build expectation, subvert twice, then deliver — is textbook comedy escalation. 'That's what exploded?' in disbelief, followed by 'That was crazy,' is exactly the right understated response. The gag earns its payoff through patience.

jokes.text: You weren't shooting, you were choking, so I had to save us. / I was going to shoot. / You always do this, every single time.
jokes.setup: Post-chase, they argue about who shot the gun
jokes.punchline: Jenko's accusation that Schmidt 'always chokes' is a callback to the prom-asking sequence; Schmidt insisting 'I was going to shoot' mirrors his insisting he was going to ask Molly out
jokes.explanation: The callback works on a thematic level — Schmidt's choking is a character trait, not situational. The parallel between asking Molly out and shooting a gun is a smart structural echo that makes both moments richer.

jokes.text: Can't believe you made me late. You're so selfish. / I'm selfish? Are you fucking kidding me? Look at yourself!
jokes.setup: Post-chase; Schmidt is upset about missing his school play
jokes.punchline: Schmidt accusing Jenko of being selfish — after Schmidt nearly sabotaged their entire investigation for a school play — is a perfect irony. Jenko's incredulity is completely justified.
jokes.explanation: The situational irony of Schmidt calling anyone selfish at this moment is very funny. The 'Look at yourself!' is especially good — Jenko gesturing at Schmidt's Peter Pan costume as if it makes the argument for him.

jokes.text: Yesterday, I found a college application on your desk! I don't know how long this case is going to last. And Eric's going to get into Berkeley, and, honestly, I can get in, too. Who knows? I could ride this thing out. I could be a doctor or something.
jokes.setup: Schmidt and Jenko are having a serious argument about the case; Schmidt goes off-script
jokes.punchline: Schmidt's argument escalates from 'I want to finish the play' to 'I could be a doctor' — revealing he has genuinely lost himself in his high school identity
jokes.explanation: This is the film's core comedic/thematic idea playing out at full volume — the undercover cop so deep in the assignment he's literally planning a fake college career. 'I could be a doctor or something' is delivered with genuine enthusiasm that's hilarious and also slightly sad. Strong character integration — this only works because of everything we've seen build to this point.

jokes.text: At least I know my Miranda rights, you idiot.
jokes.setup: Jenko tells Schmidt he's 'in too deep' and needs to remember he's a cop
jokes.punchline: His proof that he's the more grounded cop is knowing his Miranda rights — which is literally the minimum requirement of the job
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic deflation — Jenko's argument that he's the more professional cop peaks at 'at least I know my Miranda rights,' which is an almost comically low bar. The 'you idiot' tag is chef's kiss. It's self-aware about how low-functioning both of them are as cops.

jokes.text: I want to thank... Give it up to French Samuels for ably backing me up. / Fuck you, Doug! What?
jokes.setup: Schmidt arrives mid-play and immediately takes the stage back from French
jokes.punchline: His gracious 'thank you' to French — the person he's displacing — is immediately answered by French's furious 'Fuck you, Doug!'
jokes.explanation: French Samuels — who was 'in character for months' — getting immediately dumped and responding with a stage shout of 'Fuck you, Doug!' is a great character payoff. The contrast between Schmidt's gracious tone and French's completely justified fury is well-structured.

jokes.text: This is my twin. We're together in... / Get the fuck out of here.
jokes.setup: Jenko tries to get onstage by claiming to be Schmidt's twin
jokes.punchline: The drama teacher cuts him off instantly with 'Get the fuck out of here' — no hesitation, complete dismissal
jokes.explanation: The speed of the rejection is what makes it funny — Jenko doesn't even finish the sentence. The teacher's 'Get the fuck out of here' is delivered with weary authority that cuts him off perfectly.

jokes.text: I don't know, but it's already more exciting.
jokes.setup: Chaos is breaking out onstage during the school play
jokes.punchline: An audience member drily observes the chaos is an improvement on the play
jokes.explanation: A quick background joke that lands on the fourth-wall awareness that the play itself is dull. It's a minor beat — functional but not distinctive.

jokes.text: I'm not dumb! I'm smart! You think I'm stupid? You're stupid!
jokes.setup: The school play has devolved into a brawl; Jenko is fighting
jokes.punchline: In the middle of physical combat, Jenko's argument is an escalating kindergarten-level self-defense: 'I'm smart! You're stupid!'
jokes.explanation: The childishness of the insult in an adult fight is funny and very Jenko. 'You're stupid' as a combat line has a certain perfect lameness. Not high craft but delivers on character.

jokes.text: Make fun of me behind my back and everybody laughs at me? I was a loser for four years! You couldn't handle it for five minutes! Have some fairy dust, motherfucker!
jokes.setup: Schmidt confronts someone who laughed at him, mid-Peter-Pan-costume brawl
jokes.punchline: 'Have some fairy dust, motherfucker!' — an absurdist threat that only makes sense because he's in a Peter Pan costume
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best moments. The emotional speech ('I was a loser for four years') hits real thematic notes, then the punchline — 'Have some fairy dust, motherfucker!' — lands as one of the most perfectly incongruous action-movie one-liners in the film. It ONLY works in that costume, making it the highest possible character integration. The contrast between genuine vulnerability and absurdist threat is emotionally resonant AND funny. High quotability. This is comfortably above the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: I heard you call me Rain Man, you asshole!
jokes.setup: Schmidt is brawling; now turns his rage on Eric specifically
jokes.punchline: He's angry about the Rain Man comment from earlier — a callback that reveals Schmidt absolutely was listening and absolutely does give a fuck
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback — directly contradicts Schmidt's earlier 'I don't give a fuck.' The rage is proportionate to the insult (Rain Man = 'your adopted brother is a burden who can't even do math') and it's funny that this specific detail was the one that broke him.

jokes.text: Principal Dadier sucks dick!
jokes.setup: Jenko is in the middle of the onstage brawl, addressing the whole school
jokes.punchline: He uses the school-wide platform to announce the principal performs fellatio — a completely non-sequitur grievance delivered with commitment
jokes.explanation: The randomness of the principal grievance is funny, and 'Principal Dadier sucks dick!' shouted at a school assembly has situational comedy. But it's fairly low-craft — the humor is mostly in the delivery context rather than the construction.

jokes.text: And that's the end of Act Two.
jokes.setup: The school play has completely collapsed into a brawl with two undercover cops fighting their way through the cast
jokes.punchline: The drama teacher announces 'And that's the end of Act Two' — treating the total chaos as if it were a planned theatrical event
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best lines. The deadpan professionalism of announcing intermission over a full-blown riot is structurally perfect — it's the contrast between the drama teacher's theatrical composure and total surrounding chaos. Five words, maximum impact. The meta quality (it IS the end of an act, structurally) is a bonus. Exceeds the 8.0 anchor in economy and structure.

jokes.text: Is that it? You're not going to scream at us? / Nope. / I'm gonna just fire you.
jokes.setup: Schmidt and Jenko expect another explosive Dickson tirade after their spectacular failure
jokes.punchline: Dickson quietly declines to scream — 'I'm gonna just fire you' — the calm is more devastating than the screaming, and funnier for it
jokes.explanation: Smart subversion of the established Dickson-screaming-at-them pattern. The audience expects another explosion; instead, they get quiet termination. The calm delivery makes it funnier and more threatening. Character-specific: Dickson has established he goes loud, so going quiet is the scariest thing he can do. At the 8.0 anchor benchmark.

jokes.text: You know what's crazy to me is that I think that I actually thought that we were brothers.
jokes.setup: Schmidt and Jenko are splitting up after their blowup; Jenko reflects on their friendship
jokes.punchline: His realization that he 'thought they were brothers' is a sincere-sounding statement that's also funny because they've been pretending to be brothers as a cover story — he's confused his real feelings with his undercover identity
jokes.explanation: Leans more into the emotional underpinning of the film than pure comedy, but there's something funny in Jenko's confused layers — the cover and the real feeling have merged. It's a soft joke with more heart than laugh.

jokes.text: I would've tooken a bullet for you.
jokes.setup: Jenko is expressing his deep loyalty to Schmidt in an emotional moment
jokes.punchline: 'Tooken' — the malapropism undermines the sincerity of the profound declaration
jokes.explanation: Perfect character comedy through linguistic failure. 'Tooken' is not just a grammar error — it's delivered with complete sincerity in what should be a dramatic moment, which makes it funnier and oddly sweeter. The word does enormous work: it characterizes Jenko (uneducated but earnest), deflates the drama, and is instantly quotable. Very high economy — one wrong word is the entire joke.

jokes.text: Get in now. Both of you. / Why should I? / Just get in the car, man. / Get in the fucking car. / Nope, not until you ask nicely. / Please get in the car.
jokes.setup: Dickson pulls up to rehire them; they're being petulant
jokes.punchline: Jenko (or Schmidt) refuses to get in the car until asked nicely — forcing a dignified police captain to say 'please get in the car' — and Dickson actually complies
jokes.explanation: The power dynamic inversion — a subordinate demanding their superior say 'please' and getting it — is funny, especially from Ice Cube's Dickson. The escalating specificity ('not until you ask nicely' → 'Please get in the car') lands well.

jokes.text: It rhymes with 'grape'! It rhymes with 'grape.' I can't let that happen.
jokes.setup: Eric is explaining why he's afraid of going to jail; he says he's too handsome and something bad will happen to a 'handsome guy like me'
jokes.punchline: He can't say 'rape' but delivers 'it rhymes with grape' twice — the euphemism is both absurd and reveals the joke has been structured to avoid the word
jokes.explanation: The euphemism-as-structure is well-executed — 'it rhymes with grape' is said twice, which amplifies the discomfort while keeping the actual word out. The doubling of the rhyme is also funny in itself. Eric's vanity ('a handsome guy like me') framing the fear adds character specificity. Very quotable.

jokes.text: A lot of things have made me wonder about you. Your taste in music. The fact that you look like a fucking 40-year-old man. Then after that shit at the play, I realized there's no way you guys could be cops.
jokes.setup: Eric has had suspicions about Schmidt and Jenko being undercover cops
jokes.punchline: His list of suspicious things — taste in music, looking 40 — culminates in the punchline: the school play brawl in a Peter Pan costume convinced him they COULDN'T be cops. Perfect irony.
jokes.explanation: Structurally elegant: Eric lists legitimate red flags, then the event that cleared their suspicion is the most ludicrous thing they did. The joke is that incompetence and absurdity are better cover than any deliberate undercover work. 'You look like a fucking 40-year-old man' is a great specific detail. The punchline structure is clean and the irony is rich.

jokes.text: That was... That was actually really fuckin' awesome. / Beginner's luck.
jokes.setup: Schmidt fires a gun for the 'first time' (as his cover identity) and hits the target perfectly
jokes.punchline: He dismisses a perfect shot as 'beginner's luck' — an understatement that lands because we know he's a trained cop
jokes.explanation: Clean dramatic irony — Schmidt understating his trained marksmanship as 'beginner's luck' is a good undercover comedy beat. Eric's impressed reaction sets it up well.

jokes.text: Schmidty! Chore time! / Mom, we don't have time for chores right now! / If you stay in this house, you have time for chores! / Mom!
jokes.setup: Schmidt and Jenko are preparing for a major drug bust; they're at Schmidt's childhood home
jokes.punchline: His mom interrupts their tactical prep to insist on chores — the mundane domesticity is completely at odds with the life-or-death operation
jokes.explanation: Classic comedy of incongruity — the contrast between 'preparing to infiltrate a drug deal' and 'Mom wants me to do chores' is well-deployed. Schmidt's 'Mom!' at the end is both a teenager's whine and a cop's exasperation. Good character work.

jokes.text: Fuck this thing. [Schmidt struggling with equipment]
jokes.setup: Schmidt is gearing up for the prom drug bust; some piece of equipment is giving him trouble
jokes.punchline: His quiet 'Fuck this thing' — a mundane frustration during serious operation prep — is a small but real comedy beat
jokes.explanation: Minor moment — a small incongruity laugh. It's a real beat but not especially crafted. Functions as a breathing moment in the prom prep montage.

jokes.text: Here. It'll be quicker if I help. / There you go. / Thanks.
jokes.setup: Jenko and Schmidt just had a falling out; they're both getting ready for prom separately but Jenko offers to help Schmidt with his outfit
jokes.punchline: The quiet domestic tenderness of the moment — two estranged 'brothers' making peace over prom prep — played completely straight, which is funnier than any joke would be
jokes.explanation: The humor here is tonal — after a genuine fight, Jenko quietly helps Schmidt with his prom outfit as a peace offering, and both men accept the moment without irony. It's the kind of comedy that's funny because it's so earnest. The 'Thanks' is the whole punchline. Strong character integration; this only works because of everything that preceded it.

jokes.text: Your shotgun's hanging too low. They're gonna see it.
jokes.setup: Schmidt's mom is helping Jenko adjust his prom outfit; she treats the concealed shotgun as a wardrobe problem
jokes.punchline: She addresses the concealed weapon as a fashion concern — 'hanging too low' — with complete maternal practicality
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's strongest moments. The joke is in the character: Schmidt's mom treats tactical firearm concealment exactly like she'd treat an untucked shirt. The calm competence with which she addresses the shotgun's visibility — as if she regularly helps her son hide weapons for prom — is both funny and implies a rich offscreen history. Very economical. At the 8.0 anchor benchmark.

jokes.text: Jenko... Will you go to prom with me? / I guess.
jokes.setup: Schmidt and Jenko are reconciled and preparing for the prom drug bust together
jokes.punchline: Schmidt formally asks Jenko to prom — mirroring his earlier agonized invitation to Molly — and Jenko's 'I guess' is the least romantic possible acceptance
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best structural jokes. The callback to the prom-asking sequence is perfect — Schmidt's earlier five-minute ordeal of choking and stammering is now compressed into one clean, confident question to his partner. Jenko's 'I guess' is the ideal anticlimactic response: it's the opposite of Molly's enthusiastic yes, yet somehow more meaningful as a reconciliation. The buddy-movie subtext is the actual text. The structure earns maximum points — the whole reel builds to this.

jokes.text: Ms. Griggs oscillating between 'go' and 'stay' commands while Brad tries to leave — the teacher-student inappropriate relationship chaos compressed into absurd back-and-forth
jokes.setup: Brad (Jenko) has snuck into the teacher's area and Ms. Griggs is simultaneously trying to get rid of him and beg him to stay
jokes.punchline: 'Get out of me. I'm going to throw up.' followed immediately by 'You are so hot!' — the rapid emotional whiplash of someone both disgusted and attracted
jokes.explanation: The rapid-fire contradictory commands ('stay/go/stay/go') is a well-executed bit on the cringe of a forbidden attraction. The payoff 'Get out of me' is an awkward malapropism that works. Good sustained cringe but not quite exceptional.

jokes.text: Cut to Schmidt at prom — reaction shot after the chaotic teacher scene, implying a visual 'meanwhile' juxtaposition
jokes.setup: The frenetic, embarrassing Jenko/Ms. Griggs scene
jokes.punchline: Hard cut to 'All right.' — Schmidt's flat, businesslike composure contrasted with the chaos we just witnessed
jokes.explanation: Functional transition gag — the flat 'All right' after the craziness is a mild tonal contrast beat. Not much to it on its own.

jokes.text: 'Hey, pumpkin head. I'm very mad at you. Dance with me.'
jokes.setup: Schmidt/Doug has apparently wronged Molly, so she approaches him at the prom angry
jokes.punchline: Instead of confronting him, she says 'Dance with me' — the non-sequitur demand paired with 'I'm very mad at you' is a funny character contradiction
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of anger and an immediate request to dance is a genuinely funny character moment — it captures teenage illogic well. 'Pumpkin head' as an affectionate insult is a nice touch. Economical and character-specific.

jokes.text: 'Making a lot of hand gestures!'
jokes.setup: Schmidt is urgently telling Molly to leave, using emphatic hand gestures, in the middle of a prom
jokes.punchline: A random background student calls out exactly what Schmidt is doing in a completely non-contextual way, as if narrating the obvious
jokes.explanation: Four words, completely absurdist, perfectly timed. A random student simply announcing what Schmidt is doing for no reason is surreal and very funny. Its economy is exceptional — maximum laugh per syllable. This is a hallmark Lord/Miller gag: throwaway background joke that lands harder than the main action.

jokes.text: 'Okay, my name's not Doug. It's Schmidt. And I'm a cop.'
jokes.setup: Schmidt has been undercover as 'Doug' the whole film; Molly's reaction ('What?... What?') mirrors the audience's moment of dramatic revelation
jokes.punchline: Molly's repeated stunned 'What?' beats after each confession — the structure of gradually dropping bombs and each landing the same flat reaction
jokes.explanation: The two-stage reveal ('It's Schmidt' / 'What?' / 'And I'm a cop' / 'What?') is structurally solid. Each revelation gets the same dumbfounded response. Standard but competently executed.

jokes.text: Mr. Walters revealed as the drug supplier — 'You're the supplier? You're a teacher.'
jokes.setup: The mysterious drug supplier has been a major plot threat; Schmidt and Jenko arrive at the penthouse expecting a dangerous criminal
jokes.punchline: It's their dopey chemistry teacher Mr. Walters, who cheerfully explains he needed the money because of alimony
jokes.explanation: The reveal lands because Walters has been a consistent comic presence as the clueless teacher — making him the drug kingpin is a satisfying payoff. His explanation ('Could barely pay my alimony. What are you gonna do?') is perfectly nonchalant and character-consistent. Good structural use of the character.

jokes.text: Walters narrates making the drug: 'I stole some of that Bunsen burner crap from the chem lab, threw in some of my Cool Deets, and it was muy delicioso!'
jokes.setup: Walters explains his drug manufacturing process to the undercover cops as if describing a fun cooking project
jokes.punchline: 'muy delicioso!' — the casual, food-review energy applied to synthesizing illegal narcotics, plus 'Cool Deets' (his cologne brand) as an ingredient
jokes.explanation: Deeply character-specific — only Walters would describe drug synthesis with 'muy delicioso' and use his own cologne brand as an ingredient. His oblivious enthusiasm is perfectly calibrated. The callback to 'Cool Deets' rewards attentive viewers.

jokes.text: 'Then one day I catch Eco Butt-munch over here smoking a J.J. behind the field house'
jokes.setup: Walters is explaining how he recruited Eric as his distributor
jokes.punchline: 'Eco Butt-munch' as a nickname for the environmentally-conscious Eric, and 'J.J.' as his folksy term for a joint
jokes.explanation: Walters's invented slang ('J.J.' for joint, 'Eco Butt-munch') is funny character voice. It captures his particular brand of trying-too-hard coolness. 'Eco Butt-munch' as a compound insult referencing Eric's character trait is good economy.

jokes.text: 'What a green penis that guy is, huh?'
jokes.setup: Walters has just finished explaining how he recruited Eric, calling him 'Eco Butt-munch'
jokes.punchline: 'Green penis' as an invented derogatory term — the unexpected anatomical component of an eco-related insult, delivered with chummy camaraderie
jokes.explanation: This is a legitimately great character-comedy line. 'Green penis' is a totally invented insult that shouldn't work but absolutely does — the 'green' modifying 'penis' as an eco-themed put-down is bizarre and specific in the best way. Only Walters, in his oblivious bro-teacher mode, would coin this term and deploy it with zero self-awareness. Highly quotable, deeply weird, earns every point.

jokes.text: 'There's my quesadilla. I hurt my hands! Bitch.'
jokes.setup: In the middle of a tense drug deal reveal, Walters suddenly notices his quesadilla has arrived
jokes.punchline: He apparently punches or slaps something in excitement, hurts his hands, then calls his food a 'bitch' — a surreal three-beat non-sequitur in the middle of a crime scene
jokes.explanation: Three words: 'I hurt my hands!' The complete tonal derailment — from drug reveal to food excitement to self-injury to calling a quesadilla a 'bitch' — is perfectly absurdist. The sequence is economy at its best: three separate micro-jokes crammed into one beat. The 'quesadilla' callback also pays off later at 88:02.

jokes.text: Karl/gang leader's entrance: 'You guys look crazy scary. How many of you are there? A lot.'
jokes.setup: The mysterious, dangerous drug boss Karl arrives at the penthouse with his entourage
jokes.punchline: He self-assesses his own crew as 'crazy scary' then answers his own rhetorical question with the vague, dismissive 'A lot' — an intimidating crime boss being oddly casual about his own intimidation
jokes.explanation: The self-aware intimidation ('you guys look crazy scary') followed by the nonchalant 'A lot' is a good subversion of the crime-boss archetype. Understated and funny.

jokes.text: Meeting the gang leader: 'You guys look crazy scary. How many of you are there? A lot.'
jokes.setup: Walters and the boys meet the actual criminal gang
jokes.punchline: Walters's reaction ('You guys look crazy scary') followed by the flat, unhelpful 'How many of you are there? / A lot.' exchange — both characters playing it completely straight
jokes.explanation: Walters's social awkwardness with actual criminals is a good comedic beat. The 'A lot' response is funny in its non-specificity. Functional humor that characterizes both the dorky teacher-criminal and the laconic gang.

jokes.text: 'Patch looks pimp, man.' 'Thank you.'
jokes.setup: Jenko is terrified they'll be recognized by the gang; he's desperately looking for something to say
jokes.punchline: He compliments a gang member's eye patch, the gang member accepts graciously — a bizarrely wholesome exchange in a deadly tense situation
jokes.explanation: The sincerity of the exchange cuts through the tension perfectly. 'Thank you' as a straight response is the whole joke — both parties just briefly became normal people having a normal compliment exchange. Good tonal whiplash.

jokes.text: Karl: 'I don't like strangers.' Jenko: 'How do you ever expect to make any new friends with that attitude?'
jokes.setup: Karl, the terrifying drug lord, threatens Schmidt and Jenko as unknown interlopers in his drug deal
jokes.punchline: Jenko responds with earnest life-coaching advice about friendship to a murderous gang leader — the total mismatch of register
jokes.explanation: This is Jenko's character in a nutshell — his bro-philosophy delivered at maximally inappropriate moments. The sincerity of 'everyone's a stranger till you give them a chance, man' as a response to a death threat is perfectly calibrated. Karl's bewildered 'What the fuck are you talking about?' validates the audience's reaction. Excellent character integration and economy.

jokes.text: Jenko: 'It's like, everyone's a stranger till you give them a chance, man.' Karl: 'What the fuck are you talking about? I don't even...' Jenko: 'Just fuckin' around. Do your thing, man. Proceed.'
jokes.setup: Jenko has just delivered earnest friendship advice to a gang lord who is visibly confused and threatening
jokes.punchline: 'Just fuckin' around. Do your thing, man. Proceed.' — Jenko immediately backtracks with a casual 'proceed' as if he's a manager dismissing an employee, defusing the death threat with absurd professionalism
jokes.explanation: 'Proceed' is the operative word — it's Jenko pretending to be in control of a situation where he has absolutely no power. The move from genuine bro-philosophy to instant retreat to commanding 'proceed' at a crime boss is a three-stage joke that works on every level.

jokes.text: Karl recognizes Schmidt: 'You look familiar.' Schmidt: 'I was in a French fry commercial when I was a kid, so people often say they know me.'
jokes.setup: Karl suspects he's seen Schmidt before — the audience fears he'll recognize them as cops
jokes.punchline: Schmidt deflects with a totally unexpected cover story about a childhood French fry commercial, shifting from danger to absurdity
jokes.explanation: The left turn to 'French fry commercial' is a great misdirection — it relieves tension by being so random yet specific, and Schmidt commits to it fully. The setup (feared recognition) makes the absurd punchline land harder because stakes are real.

jokes.text: Karl: 'Do I look like I eat French fries?' Schmidt: 'I don't know, you look like you're in great shape, but maybe you have, like, one cheat day, like a carb blowout, you know?'
jokes.setup: Karl takes offense at the implication he eats junk food, asserting his physique
jokes.punchline: Schmidt attempts to diplomatically acknowledge Karl's physique while keeping the lie alive, devolving into speculating about his 'carb blowout' cheat day — Schmidt nervously over-explaining to a crime boss
jokes.explanation: Schmidt's social anxiety manifesting as diet-coaching a threatening crime boss is good character work. 'Carb blowout' is a funny specific detail. The escalation of an increasingly absurd cover story under pressure is classic Schmidt.

jokes.text: Schmidt performs the actual jingle: 'Come to Andrew's French Fry Emporium / Where friendship and French fries / Go hand in hand'
jokes.setup: Schmidt has committed to the French fry commercial lie; Karl is skeptical
jokes.punchline: Schmidt actually sings the full jingle, an earnest and terrible commercial tune, to prove the lie — the commitment to the bit escalates the absurdity to a breaking point
jokes.explanation: This is one of the reel's best jokes. The French fry commercial lie was already funny; Schmidt actually performing the jingle to a drug lord escalates it to absurdist heights. The jingle itself is perfectly crafted to sound like a real 1990s local commercial — 'Where friendship and French fries go hand in hand' has an earnest badness that's genuinely funny. The commitment to the bit under life-threatening circumstances is a great character-and-structure payoff. Comparable to the '8.0 anchor' level.

jokes.text: Molly bursts in: 'That's my quesadilla! Who wants a piece? Huh? I know you're in there, Doug, or whatever your name is! You lied to me! I'm gonna kill you, you stupid fucking cop!'
jokes.setup: An intense penthouse drug deal scene; Molly has stormed in, clearly on drugs, enraged at Schmidt
jokes.punchline: She opens with 'That's my quesadilla!' — an urgent food-ownership claim — before pivoting to blowing Schmidt's cover and threatening his life
jokes.explanation: This is exceptionally constructed. The quesadilla callback from Walters's earlier bit pays off perfectly — Molly bursting in to claim the food before blowing up the entire operation is a masterpiece of tonal collision. The priorities (quesadilla first, blowing cover second) are perfectly drug-addled and character-consistent. The cascade of revelations she delivers while ranting ('you stupid fucking cop') destroys everything in seconds. Among the best payoffs in the reel.

jokes.text: Jenko: 'Hey, you guys, she just called me a stupid fucking cock. That's rude.' Then: 'Did she just say "nickhead dark motherfucker"? That's just racist.'
jokes.setup: Molly is screaming 'stupid fucking cop' and 'dickhead narc motherfucker' at Schmidt and Jenko in front of the drug lord
jokes.punchline: Jenko misheats her as saying 'stupid fucking cock' and 'nickhead dark motherfucker' — his selective hearing turning a cover-blowing crisis into mild social grievances about rudeness and racism
jokes.explanation: This is the reel's standout joke. The structure is perfect: Molly screams two obscenities that contain the words 'cop' and 'narc' (which will get them killed), and Jenko mishears BOTH in ways that completely miss the actual threat but create new social complaints ('that's rude' / 'that's just racist'). The specificity of the mishearing ('nickhead dark motherfucker') is brilliantly constructed — it sounds enough like the original to be a plausible hearing error. His prioritization of social etiquette over imminent death is peak Jenko. Approaches the 9+ anchor territory for character comedy in an action context.

jokes.text: Eric reacts to learning they're cops: 'But we partied together, man. You bought us Taco Bell.'
jokes.setup: Eric's drug operation is busted; Schmidt and Jenko are revealed as cops
jokes.punchline: Eric's betrayal reaction focuses entirely on the Taco Bell purchase as the ultimate breach of trust — as if fast food generosity creates an unbreakable social contract
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Taco Bell' as the measure of friendship sincerity is a perfect choice — it's both extremely specific and extremely low-stakes, making Eric's devastation funnier. The idea that buying someone fast food creates a bond you can't betray by being an undercover cop is teenage logic at its finest. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Schmidt: 'Eric, honestly, that was a sincere gesture.' Eric: 'You made me this friendship bracelet.' 'Well, he's not really your friend. He was pretending the whole time.' Schmidt: 'I'm gonna cut this the fuck off later, all right?'
jokes.setup: Eric is heartbroken about the friendship bracelet Schmidt made him; Schmidt is trying to manage the arrest situation
jokes.punchline: Schmidt's guilt-ridden promise to 'cut this the fuck off later' — he's simultaneously arresting someone and managing the emotional fallout of a fake friendship, with the bracelet becoming a symbol of his genuine discomfort
jokes.explanation: The hostage negotiation / friendship therapy blend is very good. Schmidt's 'I'm gonna cut this the fuck off later' has the energy of someone making a dental appointment — it's a promise to deal with uncomfortable feelings later while dealing with a more urgent crisis. Good cringe-comedy with genuine emotional underpinning.

jokes.text: Karl takes Molly hostage. 'Trying to take a hostage, some goddamn TV show shit?' / 'I don't know! I'm trying to help, all right? I've never done this shit before.' / 'Well, you're fucking up.'
jokes.setup: Karl grabs Molly as a human shield — a standard action movie trope
jokes.punchline: His own henchman D.B. criticizes him for the cliché ('some goddamn TV show shit'); Karl admits he's improvising and D.B. coldly evaluates his performance ('Well, you're fucking up')
jokes.explanation: A masterfully self-aware beat. The crime boss taking a hostage is immediately critiqued by his own associate for being clichéd, and his vulnerable admission 'I've never done this shit before' humanizes him at the worst possible moment. D.B.'s clinical 'Well, you're fucking up' as performance review for hostage-taking is the perfect deadpan cap. This is exactly the kind of meta-awareness that made 21 Jump Street's comedy distinctive.

jokes.text: Eric: 'Drop your guns, or I'll spray her brains all over the room!' / Crime boss: 'Trying to take a hostage, some goddamn TV show shit?'
jokes.setup: Eric, the student drug dealer, tries to take Molly hostage
jokes.punchline: The hardened crime boss immediately identifies Eric's hostage move as clichéd 'TV show shit' — the film mocking its own genre conventions through a criminal character
jokes.explanation: The meta-commentary works because it's delivered by a character, not the film directly. Having the crime boss be a connoisseur of genre conventions while in the middle of a crime is a clever self-aware beat. Fits the film's overall self-referential tone.

jokes.text: 'Drop your guns or she's dead.' / 'She looks dead already.' / 'What? No. Jesus. Yeah, I can hear her breathing. She just passed out from the drugs. We're good.'
jokes.setup: Karl is using unconscious Molly as a hostage; Schmidt and Jenko are pretending to comply
jokes.punchline: Schmidt offhandedly notes 'She looks dead already,' causing Karl to defensively check and confirm she's just passed out — the hostage-taker reassuring the hostage's friends that she's alive
jokes.explanation: Role reversal joke executed perfectly: the person being threatened into compliance forces the threatening party to defend the value of the hostage. 'We're good' as Karl's conclusion after checking on Molly's vital signs is a great absurd payoff — he's accidentally become the most invested party in Molly's wellbeing.

jokes.text: Schmidt and Jenko drop their guns in 'good faith'; Karl immediately has them shot at. Schmidt: 'Oh, come on, that's unfair! We put our guns down in good faith. You're a liar, and you're mean!'
jokes.setup: Schmidt and Jenko have surrendered their weapons as negotiated; Karl immediately tries to have them killed
jokes.punchline: Schmidt's response to attempted murder is 'that's unfair' and 'you're mean' — the vocabulary of a playground dispute applied to being shot at
jokes.explanation: Schmidt's social register (appeals to fairness, moral condemnation) versus the actual stakes (being shot) is a consistent and excellent joke structure for this character. 'You're a liar, and you're mean' in response to an assassination attempt is funny because it's so small and correct — morally true but tonally absurd. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Jenko: 'We're all friends here. Let's just relax, and we can all leave here as friends.' / 'Yeah, let's do that.'
jokes.setup: They're being shot at after their guns are taken
jokes.punchline: Jenko sincerely pitches a 'leave as friends' resolution to a gunfight, and Schmidt immediately co-signs it — both acting as if this is a viable diplomatic outcome
jokes.explanation: Continuation of Jenko's 'everyone can be friends' philosophy at peak absurdity. Schmidt's immediate agreement ('Yeah, let's do that') is good partner-comedy. Slight repetition of earlier friendship-advice beats reduces freshness.

jokes.text: Schmidt and Jenko: 'Oh, my God, we're gonna die. We're gonna die.'
jokes.setup: Guns are drawn from all sides; the situation is hopeless
jokes.punchline: Both cops, in unison, flatly announcing their impending deaths — no heroics, no plan, just shared resignation
jokes.explanation: The synchronized resignation reads as good partner-comedy — they've synced up enough to panic in tandem. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: DEA agents burst in — Tom Hanson and Doug Penhall — from the original 21 Jump Street TV show. 'Tom Hanson, DEA! On your knees!'
jokes.setup: Schmidt and Jenko are about to die; a rescue arrives
jokes.punchline: The rescuers are Tom Hanson and Doug Penhall — the actors from the original 1980s TV show, whose character names Schmidt and Jenko have been using as aliases throughout the film
jokes.explanation: This is an exceptional meta-joke that works on multiple levels simultaneously: it's a rescue scene, a cameo from the original show's stars (Johnny Depp and Peter DeLuise), a payoff to the aliases Schmidt and Jenko have been using all film, and a commentary on the franchise itself. The audience who knows the original show gets a 9/10 joke; those who don't still get a funny reveal. This is exactly the kind of joke that becomes a cultural reference point for the film. Approaches 9+ territory.

jokes.text: Hanson to Jenko/Schmidt: 'You played saxophone at my sister's wedding, man!' Penhall: 'Tough titty. I fucked her, too.'
jokes.setup: Jenko recognizes Hanson/Penhall from before; there's a brief human connection moment
jokes.punchline: 'Tough titty. I fucked her, too.' — Penhall's completely unhinged, sociopathic response to a moment of connection destroys the warmth instantly
jokes.explanation: 'Tough titty. I fucked her, too.' is a perfect economy joke — maximum shock per syllable. Coming from a character who just made a human connection, the pivot to casual sexual disclosure is an effective dark-comedy gut-punch. The original TV cast being willing to say this amplifies the meta-joke.

jokes.text: Hanson's rant about the fake nose: 'Do you see this nose? That is a fake nose. Do you want to wear a fake nose on your fuckin' head for, like, months on end? Glue and shit?'
jokes.setup: Hanson/Penhall are scolding Schmidt and Jenko for ruining a five-year investigation
jokes.punchline: Hanson's legitimate grievances are entirely about the physical discomfort of wearing a prosthetic nose for months — the indignity of undercover work reduced to the specific horror of adhesive nose glue
jokes.explanation: The specificity of the nose-glue complaint is the joke — a veteran DEA agent with five years of work ruined, and his primary concern is 'glue and shit' on his face. Good character comedy through misdirected priorities.

jokes.text: Penhall: 'We had to get fuckin' tattoos on our dicks, man.' Then immediately: 'Hey, actually, I just said that to mess with you.'
jokes.setup: Hanson has listed undercover hardships; Penhall one-ups with a penis tattoo claim
jokes.punchline: He immediately reveals he made it up just to mess with them — the casual cruelty of inventing penile suffering as a prank
jokes.explanation: Two-beat joke with a clean structure: shocking claim, immediate deflation. The move to invent penile suffering purely for the pleasure of messing with someone is good character comedy for Penhall. The casualness of 'I just said that to mess with you' is funnier than the original claim.

jokes.text: Schmidt: 'Metro Police, Jump Street Division.' Hanson: 'Come on, you guys are Jump Street?' / 'That's funny, because we were actually Jump Street.'
jokes.setup: Schmidt identifies their unit to the DEA agents
jokes.punchline: The original Jump Street officers reveal they originated the program — connecting the film explicitly to its TV source material with a knowing wink
jokes.explanation: A satisfying meta-loop: the guys who were the original Jump Street program encountering the guys using their identities in the Jump Street program. Good structural comedy, strong reward for franchise-aware audience.

jokes.text: Two random prom students observe the gunfight: 'That was a gun.' / 'Somebody definitely got shot.'
jokes.setup: A gun has been fired in the middle of the prom
jokes.punchline: Two background students calmly process the event with the most understated possible analysis — forensic certainty delivered in the flattest possible tone
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical background comedy in the Lord/Miller tradition (echoes the 'Making a lot of hand gestures!' joke). The flat, investigative certainty of 'Somebody definitely got shot' at a prom gunfight is surreal and funny. Excellent economy.

jokes.text: Jenko mid-chase: 'Did I hit anything?' Schmidt: 'You were shooting at the fuckin' ceiling.'
jokes.setup: They're in the middle of a chaotic gunfight escape
jokes.punchline: Jenko's honest inquiry about his marksmanship, answered with the revelation that he was aiming at architecture
jokes.explanation: Good tight exchange. Jenko's earnest inquiry followed by Schmidt's flat correction — the ceiling as target is funnier than any miss could be. Good economy and character voice.

jokes.text: Jenko's emotional confession to Schmidt during the gunfight: 'I know sometimes I was a jerk to you when we were undercover... I didn't feel good about myself. All that stuff I wore, like the bracelets, the rings, the tight pants, was just so that people would think I'm cool. The only approval I ever needed was my best friend.'
jokes.setup: They're literally in the middle of a dangerous situation with multiple armed criminals
jokes.punchline: Jenko chooses this exact moment for a lengthy heartfelt emotional apology and confession — timing an intimate friendship moment in a gunfight
jokes.explanation: The joke is good (wrong time for confessional) but runs slightly long. The emotional sincerity works for character development but the comedic premise (inappropriate timing) overstays slightly. The beats about 'bracelets, rings, tight pants' are good specific details.

jokes.text: Jenko: 'Let's make a baby.' Schmidt: 'What? What are you talking about?' Jenko: 'I don't know. I was trying to sound cool. Sorry.'
jokes.setup: They're about to chase down the escaping criminals — a moment calling for a cool action line
jokes.punchline: Jenko's attempt at a badass rally cry produces 'Let's make a baby' — immediately recognized as wrong, explained with disarming honesty
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best character jokes. Jenko attempts to deliver an action-hero line and produces 'Let's make a baby' — the gap between intention and output is perfectly Jenko. His immediate self-awareness ('I don't know. I was trying to sound cool. Sorry.') is funnier than the original misfire. The apology makes it. Very high quotability and character integration — only Jenko would do this and immediately admit defeat.

jokes.text: Background prom attendee, completely delighted: 'That was crazy! You killed a guy!'
jokes.setup: A car chase has apparently crashed through/near the prom
jokes.punchline: A student's response to witnessing what appears to be a murder is unhinged enthusiasm rather than horror
jokes.explanation: Good background comedy — the unearned excitement about witnessing violence is funny. Part of the film's consistent joke about high schoolers' detachment from danger. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: Jenko and Schmidt do a stunt/car flip and immediately discuss how cool it looked: 'Did it look cool when I did it?' / 'That's what I'm talking about!'
jokes.setup: They've just executed a dangerous driving stunt in pursuit of criminals
jokes.punchline: Their immediate post-stunt concern is aesthetics — not safety, not the chase, but whether the move looked cool
jokes.explanation: Classic action-movie deconstruction — the heroes caring about how they look rather than the mission. 'Did it look cool when I did it?' is a good line because of its simplicity and earnestness. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Car stunt landing — 'You want to drive? / Yeah, I do, actually / Okay, cool. / Nice! Did it look cool when I did it? / That's what I'm talking about! Yeah!'
jokes.setup: An action sequence involving a car stunt
jokes.punchline: Instead of post-action toughness, they immediately devolve into mutual compliments about how cool it looked — like kids who just did a skateboard trick
jokes.explanation: The deflation of action-movie coolness with 'Did it look cool when I did it?' captures the film's buddy-comedy core. Character-specific and warm. Not the strongest joke but serves the relationship dynamics.

jokes.text: Jenko hanging out the car window at pursuers: 'How you guys doing back there, huh? God, I love high school! Best prom night ever!'
jokes.setup: They're being shot at during a car chase at prom
jokes.punchline: Jenko's response is to socialize with the gunmen and declare this a great prom experience — his high-school values entirely undimmed by the mortal danger
jokes.explanation: 'Best prom night ever!' during an active shooter situation is a good character joke — Jenko evaluating life experiences by high-school social metrics. Perfectly in character and economical.

jokes.text: 'Hey, you got a gun. Why don't you shoot back there? Shoot that gun, shoot that gun!' / 'All right, one second!' / 'Just shoot someone, you bitch!'
jokes.setup: During the chase, the henchmen are trying to shoot at their pursuers
jokes.punchline: 'Just shoot someone, you bitch!' — the exasperated, petulant demand from one criminal to another, 'someone' being the operative non-specific word
jokes.explanation: 'Just shoot someone' is a good criminal-management line — the low bar of 'anyone will do' as performance standard. The 'you bitch' escalation makes it land.

jokes.text: Eric emerges from the sunroof: 'Peek-a-boo! Give me my money! Fuck that! Fuck that! No! No! I can't do this! I'm supposed to go to Berkeley!'
jokes.setup: Eric, the eco-activist drug dealer, pops out during the car chase armed
jokes.punchline: 'I can't do this! I'm supposed to go to Berkeley!' — his criminal resolve collapsing mid-action into the reveal that he had a legitimate college future, which makes his drug dealing even more pathetic and funny
jokes.explanation: Excellent character payoff. 'I'm supposed to go to Berkeley!' mid-shootout is the perfect deflation of Eric's criminal persona — he's fundamentally a good student who made terrible choices. The escalation from 'Peek-a-boo' bravado to immediate collapse to Berkeley revelation is a great three-stage joke. Highly quotable and character-specific.

jokes.text: Jenko hanging out of the sunroof: 'I'm gonna get the party started! I'm gonna get the party started!' — while actively in a gunfight
jokes.setup: Jenko is in a dangerous car chase/gunfight
jokes.punchline: He announces his participation in a gunfight using party-starting rhetoric, treating gun violence as social event facilitation
jokes.explanation: Consistent Jenko character work — high-school social frame applied to violence. Works but isn't as sharp as his best moments this reel.

jokes.text: Jenko hanging from the limo sunroof: 'Hey, I'm living my dream of standing in a limo!' — while being dragged at high speed
jokes.setup: Jenko is in mortal danger, being dragged by or hanging from a moving vehicle
jokes.punchline: He pauses to acknowledge that this fulfills a specific dream of his — standing in a limo — as if the life-threatening context is beside the point
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best lines. 'Hey, I'm living my dream of standing in a limo!' is a perfect Jenko encapsulation — his life goals are so specifically low-stakes that achieving one during a gunfight is both hilarious and strangely poignant. The specificity ('standing in') rather than 'riding in' is a great detail. Excellent economy and character integration. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Schmidt to a persistent woman on the limo: 'You're really hot and you're really slutty and it's awesome, but I got to shoot people right now!' Woman: 'You think I'm hot?'
jokes.setup: A woman in the limo keeps distracting Schmidt during a gunfight
jokes.punchline: Schmidt delivers the most honest possible compliment/dismissal ('hot and slutty... it's awesome, but...'), and she only registers the compliment — selective hearing about attractiveness during a firefight
jokes.explanation: Good two-beat joke. Schmidt's formulation is hilariously complete ('hot... slutty... awesome, but...') and her single-word response ('You think I'm hot?') is the perfect selective processing. Good economy and tonal contrast.

jokes.text: The woman falls from the vehicle, calls to the chase: 'Wait, guys! Call me! Let me know where you're ending up later.'
jokes.setup: Lisa has been ejected from the vehicle mid-chase
jokes.punchline: She treats the high-speed ejection as a normal party departure, requesting to be kept in the social loop
jokes.explanation: 'Let me know where you're ending up later' as the response to being ejected from a car chase is good deadpan. She's maintained her social priorities throughout.

jokes.text: Schmidt: 'What do you get when lithium batteries react to potassium nitrate? That would be a covalent bond, brother. That's when two atoms, they share electrons. You see, they both need what the other one has. That makes them stick together.' Jenko: 'Are you saying we're covalent bonds?' Schmidt: 'What? No. We're not atoms, dude.'
jokes.setup: Schmidt explains his improvised bomb plan; uses a chemistry metaphor that sounds like a friendship metaphor
jokes.punchline: Jenko hears the covalent bond explanation as an emotional metaphor for their partnership; Schmidt's immediate dismissal ('We're not atoms, dude') deflates the moment
jokes.explanation: This is beautifully constructed. Schmidt explains real chemistry (covalent bonds), and the language of chemistry accidentally maps perfectly onto the friendship metaphor — 'they both need what the other one has, that makes them stick together.' Jenko's earnest emotional reading ('Are you saying we're covalent bonds?') and Schmidt's flat denial ('We're not atoms, dude') is a perfect two-beat payoff. The joke works on three levels: chemistry explanation, unintended friendship metaphor, and Schmidt's annoyed deflation. Among the reel's best-structured jokes.

jokes.text: The Molotov cocktail is supposed to explode but produces tequila: 'What's this? / Tequila? / I don't know, it was supposed to explode. / Oh, shit! [It then explodes]
jokes.setup: Schmidt has built what he believes is an improvised explosive from chemistry knowledge
jokes.punchline: It first produces tequila (anticlimactic), then immediately explodes after all — delayed beat payoff
jokes.explanation: The double-beat misdirection (anticlimactic tequila, then actual explosion) is a standard comedic structure but well-executed. The delay between 'I don't know, it was supposed to explode' and the explosion is timed well for a visual comedy beat.

jokes.text: Schmidt after the explosion: 'Where'd you learn how to do that, man?' Jenko: 'App chemistry, bitch.'
jokes.setup: The explosion worked; Schmidt is impressed
jokes.punchline: 'App chemistry, bitch.' — Jenko reveals his bomb-making was entirely sourced from a smartphone app, delivered with maximum swagger
jokes.explanation: Three words, maximum economy. 'App chemistry, bitch' is a perfectly constructed boast — it's simultaneously self-deprecating (he used an app) and swaggering ('bitch'). The gap between the confidence of delivery and the mundane source is the joke. Jenko-specific, highly quotable, and a great punctuation mark for the action beat. Approaches 8+ anchor quality for economy alone.

jokes.text: Jenko shot: 'Are you okay?' Schmidt: 'You shot my partner, you motherfucker!' Karl: 'I didn't mean to shoot you! I meant to shoot him!'
jokes.setup: Karl shoots someone; everyone assesses the situation
jokes.punchline: Karl's defense is that he intended to shoot someone else — the criminal ethic where intent to commit a different murder is apparently exculpatory
jokes.explanation: 'I didn't mean to shoot you! I meant to shoot him!' is a great misapplication of moral logic — as if intending a different target excuses the shooting entirely. The indignation in the delivery makes it funnier. Good economy.

jokes.text: Shot Jenko to Schmidt: 'Yeah, I'm feeling a little ambivalent about that right now.' (about taking a bullet for Schmidt)
jokes.setup: Schmidt asks if Jenko is okay after being shot; notes that Jenko took a bullet for him
jokes.punchline: 'I'm feeling a little ambivalent about that right now' — a measured, intellectualized response to being shot while performing a heroic act
jokes.explanation: 'Ambivalent' is exactly the right word delivered at exactly the right moment. Jenko's choice of a college-essay vocabulary word while bleeding is perfect character comedy — his attempt at emotional sophistication while in physical distress. The word's accuracy (he genuinely is conflicted about having saved Schmidt) makes it funnier. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Schmidt shoots Mr. Walters in the genitals. 'I shot him in the dick.' / 'You shot me in the dick!'
jokes.setup: Schmidt confronts Mr. Walters who is trying to escape
jokes.punchline: Schmidt shoots Walters in the penis — the film's climactic villain defeat via genital wound, confirmed in stereo by both shooter and victim
jokes.explanation: The mutual announcement ('I shot him' / 'You shot me') is perfect — both parties confirming the same fact from opposite perspectives, as if filing a report. The specific location of the wound for the mild-mannered chemistry teacher villain is an inspired choice. Walters's outrage ('You shot me in the dick!') reads as more offended than pained, which is funnier.

jokes.text: Schmidt celebrates by screaming 'Yes! Yes! Yes!' while reading Miranda rights, mixing the arrest protocol with jubilation
jokes.setup: Schmidt has just shot Walters and is placing him under arrest
jokes.punchline: He delivers the Miranda rights while simultaneously cheering — the bureaucratic formula of rights-reading intercut with victory screaming
jokes.explanation: Good juxtaposition — the formal legal language of Miranda rights punctuated by ecstatic celebration. The 'You have the right to remain silent!' gaining new subtext when delivered by someone screaming in triumph is good structural comedy.

jokes.text: Walters: 'It definitely came out my asshole!' — mid-Miranda-rights
jokes.setup: Walters has been shot in the genitals; Schmidt is reading him his rights
jokes.punchline: Walters provides real-time wound progression updates during his arrest — the bullet has apparently traveled
jokes.explanation: Perfect escalation of the genital-wound joke. Walters announcing the bullet's trajectory mid-arrest, with the precision of a medical update, is a great callback. The specificity of 'came out my asshole' as anatomical reporting rather than complaint is very funny. Excellent economy.

jokes.text: Jenko to Schmidt, post-arrest: 'You just shot him in the dick. I've never seen that. Who does that?'
jokes.setup: They've just successfully completed their mission; Jenko is debriefing emotionally
jokes.punchline: Jenko's highest form of admiration is bewildered disbelief at the genital marksmanship — 'Who does that?' as the ultimate compliment
jokes.explanation: 'Who does that?' as a form of reverent compliment is good character voice. Jenko's admiration expressed through total bewilderment is consistent and funny.

jokes.text: Jenko's escalating friendship compliments to Schmidt: '...you're sincere and you're sweet and you're loyal... And I fuckin' cherish you.'
jokes.setup: Jenko is apologizing to Schmidt and listing his virtues
jokes.punchline: 'And I fuckin' cherish you.' — the escalation of heartfelt adjectives climaxes with the most tender possible word ('cherish') delivered with a profanity ('fuckin'') that simultaneously undercuts and amplifies the sincerity
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best character jokes. 'I fuckin' cherish you' is a masterwork of tonal collision — the profanity before 'cherish' makes the tender word hit harder, not softer. It's entirely Jenko: he doesn't have the emotional vocabulary for straightforward warmth, so he swears into sincerity. The word 'cherish' is specifically funny because it's so unexpectedly formal and romantic. Highly quotable. This approaches the 8+ anchor threshold.

jokes.text: 'Should we high-five?' — followed by an apparent failed or awkward high-five attempt given Jenko is shot
jokes.setup: Jenko has just delivered an emotional declaration of friendship ('I fuckin' cherish you')
jokes.punchline: 'Should we high-five?' — the emotional moment deflated to its physical resolution option, which is immediately complicated by the fact that Jenko is wounded
jokes.explanation: The deflation of the emotional peak to 'should we high-five?' is perfectly calibrated. It doesn't undermine the sincerity — it channels it into the only physical language these characters know. Followed immediately by 'My hand!' (Jenko's wound) which is an additional beat. Very economical.

jokes.text: 'I got to get my dick sewn back on.' / 'You shut the fuck up.' / 'That's not funny.'
jokes.setup: Post-arrest, the villain is apparently holding his severed genitalia
jokes.punchline: His matter-of-fact 'I got to get my dick sewn back on' as a practical concern, Schmidt's refusal to engage with it, and Schmidt's 'That's not funny' — which is both wrong and funny
jokes.explanation: Schmidt saying 'That's not funny' about an objectively funny situation is a good ironic beat. The logistical concern of getting a dick 'sewn back on' treated as a reasonable medical errand is committed grotesque comedy.

jokes.text: Mr. Walters mid-injury: 'I got to get my dick sewn back on.' Schmidt: 'You shut the fuck up.' Then: 'That's my dick! Pick up my dick! Please!' / 'No, we're not picking up your dick.' / 'Fuckin' pick my dick up!'
jokes.setup: Walters has been shot in the genitals and is apparently in a critical medical situation
jokes.punchline: Walters escalates from a reasonable medical request ('sew it back on') to discovering a severed body part and desperately pleading for someone to retrieve it; the cops refuse with normal social disgust
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation of the genital-wound running gag. The three-party negotiation over whether to retrieve the severed appendage is structurally great: Walters pleads with increasing desperation, Schmidt categorically refuses, and the cops' normal social revulsion at the request ('No, we're not picking up your dick') is funnier than any grosser reaction would be. 'Fuckin' pick my dick up!' with the please-then-profanity structure is very quotable. This is the culmination of a well-sustained running gag.

jokes.text: Jenko to Eric as he's arrested: 'He's my friend. They don't serve vegan in jail, bitch.'
jokes.setup: Jenko is arresting Eric, who he formed a genuine connection with as a fellow popular kid during the undercover assignment
jokes.punchline: 'They don't serve vegan in jail, bitch.' — a farewell that's simultaneously friendly ('He's my friend') and a devastating practical reality check delivered as a taunt
jokes.explanation: This is the reel's best single line. 'They don't serve vegan in jail, bitch' is a masterclass in economy and character integration. It's: (1) a callback to Eric's eco-vegan identity, (2) an accurate practical threat about prison cuisine, (3) delivered as a taunt by someone who genuinely considers Eric a friend, (4) punctuated with 'bitch' in a way that's affectionately ruthless. The setup ('He's my friend') makes the pivot to the vegan threat funnier by establishing the warmth before the knife. This approaches the Snip-snap anchor territory for character-specific, quotable, economical comedy.

jokes.text: Schmidt to Molly: 'I think it's good you're mad at me. I think you should be mad at more guys, because you deserve a guy who's good and who doesn't lie to you... There are good guys out there who aren't assholes like me.'
jokes.setup: Schmidt is trying to apologize sincerely to Molly for deceiving her
jokes.punchline: 'There are good guys out there who aren't assholes like me.' — his self-deprecating conclusion accidentally argues himself out of being the good guy while trying to be the good guy
jokes.explanation: Good character-comedy moment — Schmidt's earnest attempt at a good-guy speech undermines itself. The logic spiral of 'I'm a good guy who's telling you to find a good guy who's better than me' is nicely self-defeating. Slightly diluted by the genuine emotional sincerity of the scene.

jokes.text: Molly: 'Thanks for saving my life, asshole.'
jokes.setup: Schmidt has delivered a sincere apology; Molly is processing it
jokes.punchline: 'Thanks for saving my life, asshole.' — the warmth and the insult delivered simultaneously, the affectionate 'asshole' confirming that his apology was received
jokes.explanation: Five words that contain forgiveness and resentment simultaneously — good economy. 'Asshole' as the affectionate closer is a well-worn structure but executed cleanly here.

jokes.text: Jenko to Schmidt: 'We're, like, in the end of Die Hard right now, but it's our actual life. It's crazy.' Schmidt: 'Number one or two?' Jenko: 'Three. Sam Jackson one. Yeah!'
jokes.setup: They've survived the climax of a dramatic action sequence
jokes.punchline: Jenko frames their real experience through Die Hard references, and Schmidt immediately engages in a franchise ranking debate — the action movie fan using genre knowledge to process actual action
jokes.explanation: Good meta-awareness — the characters experiencing an action movie trope and immediately curating which specific action movie it resembles. 'Three. Sam Jackson one. Yeah!' as enthusiastic franchise taxonomy is good character comedy for action-movie obsessives. The specificity (Die Hard 3 with Samuel L. Jackson, not just 'Die Hard') is a good detail.

jokes.text: Captain Dickson's speech: '...you crazy, sick, vigilante motherfuckers... Since you two cowboys love to drink booze, smoke weed with kids, and fuck anything with a big ass in jeans with low self-esteem, I'm gonna send you to a place where all that shit is allowed.'
jokes.setup: Dickson is ostensibly congratulating Schmidt and Jenko on their first arrest while also reprimanding their methods
jokes.punchline: His list of their misconduct ('smoke weed with kids... fuck anything with a big ass in jeans with low self-esteem') is so specific and detailed that the reprimand becomes a vivid appreciation of their chaos
jokes.explanation: Dickson's character-consistent rant is good writing — 'fuck anything with a big ass in jeans with low self-esteem' is a weirdly specific behavioral profile that doubles as a character description. Good character integration for Dickson whose insults are always lovingly detailed.

jokes.text: Schmidt: 'Oh, I love Disneyland!' Dickson: 'You two sons of bitches are going to college!'
jokes.setup: Dickson promises to send them 'to a place where all that shit is allowed'
jokes.punchline: Schmidt guesses Disneyland; it's college — the misdirection works because both are age-inappropriate destinations and college is somehow even funnier than the guess
jokes.explanation: One of the reel's best structural jokes and a great button for the film's climax. The setup ('a place where all that shit is allowed') creates expectation; Schmidt's guess (Disneyland) is funny and character-appropriate; the actual answer (college) is funnier because it's: (a) a sequel setup, (b) even more accurate than Disneyland re: the described behaviors, and (c) delivered with Dickson's maximum disappointment energy. Schmidt's simultaneous 'Yes!' and Jenko's 'No!' reaction perfectly captures the partners' different values. Excellent economy and structure.

jokes.text: Post-credits: 'Oh, my God! You're like two Hardy Boys in one!'
jokes.setup: Post-credits scene, apparently introducing a new character who encounters Schmidt and Jenko
jokes.punchline: 'Two Hardy Boys in one' — describing the duo as a single, combined Hardy Boy, which is both a compliment and a reduction
jokes.explanation: Light post-credits joke. The Hardy Boys reference is a reasonable fit for two young-looking undercover cops but doesn't have strong setup or character integration. Functional.

jokes.text: Final line: 'Hey, why are you here, Scott? What, Kennedy High isn't having any parties tonight?'
jokes.setup: Post-credits tag; someone named Scott appears at what is apparently a college party
jokes.punchline: The question implies Scott is too young/should be at a high school party — setting up the college assignment premise with a dig at someone's age or social standing
jokes.explanation: Setup for the sequel premise. Mild joke about someone looking too young to be at college — foreshadowing that Schmidt and Jenko will face similar issues. Functional but not strong as a standalone joke.
